cards.bridge: In §14.12, optical reversibility (Stokes' relations) proves that if denser reflection has a π phase shift, rarer reflection has none.

cards.label: 03 · §14.11 Definition
cards.title: What is Lloyd's mirror arrangement?
cards.body: Lloyd's mirror interferes direct light from slit S₁ with light reflected at grazing incidence from a mirror; its dark central fringe proves a π phase shift on denser reflection.

cards.title: Running a reflected and refracted ray backward in time
cards.meaning: Stokes' relations come from running light backward: reversing the reflected and transmitted rays must rebuild the original incident ray and cancel any extra ray.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="14" y1="90" x2="118" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="142" y1="90" x2="246" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="26" y1="42" x2="66" y2="90" class="ik"/><line x1="66" y1="90" x2="106" y2="42" class="lk"/><line x1="66" y1="90" x2="96" y2="144" class="lk"/><line x1="234" y1="42" x2="194" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="224" y1="144" x2="194" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="194" y1="90" x2="154" y2="42" class="ik"/><line x1="194" y1="90" x2="164" y2="144" class="gk"/><text x="32" y="36" class="t">a</text><text x="102" y="36" class="t">ar₁</text><text x="98" y="152" class="t">at₁</text><text x="24" y="80" class="t">n₁</text><text x="24" y="106" class="t">n₂</text><text x="148" y="32" class="t">ar₁²+at₁t₂ = a</text><text x="144" y="162" class="t">at₁r₂+ar₁t₁ = 0</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare (a) on the left (incident ray a splits into ar₁ and at₁) with time-reversed (b) on the right (rebuilds a and cancels to 0 in n₂).
cards.example: Cancelling the unwanted downward ray in medium n₂ gives at₁r₂ + ar₁t₁ = 0, so r₂ = -r₁.
cards.bridge: Since r₂ = -r₁, the opposite signs mean a π phase shift on denser reflection and zero phase shift on rarer reflection.

cards.label: 04 · §14.12 Definition
cards.title: What are Stokes' relations?
cards.body: Stokes' relations are t₁t₂ = 1 - r₁² and r₂ = -r₁, derived from optical reversibility for amplitude reflection (r₁, r₂) and transmission (t₁, t₂) coefficients.

cards.label: 05 · §14.12 Derivation
cards.title: Stokes' relations from optical reversibility
cards.legend: Incident amplitude \(a\), reflection and transmission coefficients \(r_1, t_1\) (from \(n_1\) to \(n_2\)) and \(r_2, t_2\) (from \(n_2\) to \(n_1\)) (Eqs. 14.38–14.39, Fig. 14.22).

phases.name: Retrace incident
phases.why: reversing ar₁ and at₁ must reconstruct incident amplitude a

phases.name: First Stokes law
phases.why: divide by a and isolate t₁t₂

phases.name: Cancel second ray
phases.why: equate the net amplitude along the absent direction in n₂ to zero

phases.name: Second Stokes law
phases.why: divide by a t₁ to obtain r₂ = -r₁

steps.note: By optical reversibility, reversed rays \(ar_1^2\) and \(at_1 t_2\) combine to give \(a\) (Fig. 14.22b).
Divide both sides by incident amplitude \(a\).

ask.q: Which principle states that reversed rays retrace the original path?
ask.why: In the absence of absorption, time-reversal invariance ensures optical reversibility.

steps.note: Subtract \(r_1^2\) to obtain the first Stokes' relation (Eq. 14.38).

move.label: Equate reversed amplitudes in medium 2 to zero

steps.note: In medium \(n_2\), rays \(at_1 r_2\) and \(ar_1 t_1\) must cancel completely.

ask.q: Why must \(at_1 r_2 + ar_1 t_1\) equal zero in Fig. 14.22(b)?
options: No such ray existed in Fig. 14.22(a)
ask.why: Time reversal of Fig. 14.22(a) has no outgoing ray along that direction in medium \(n_2\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(at_1\).

ask.q: Which common factor is divided out of \(at_1 r_2 + ar_1 t_1 = 0\)?
ask.why: Both terms contain the non-zero transmitted amplitude \(at_1\).

steps.note: Subtract \(r_1\) to obtain the second Stokes' relation (Eq. 14.39).

ask.q: Since denser reflection has a \(\pi\) phase shift, what does \(r_2 = -r_1\) imply for rarer reflection?
ask.why: The minus sign accounts for the \(\pi\) shift on the denser side, so the rarer side has zero shift.

cards.label: 06 · §14.10 Examples
cards.title: Mica sheet thickness from fringe shift (Examples 14.10–14.11)
cards.body: For \(n = 1.58, d = 0.1\text{ cm}, D = 50\text{ cm}, \Delta = 0.2\text{ cm}\), \(t \approx 6.7 \times 10^{-4}\text{ cm}\). If the central fringe shifts to the 11th bright fringe, \(0.58t = 11\lambda\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Why is the central fringe in Young's experiment white when white light is used?
options: All wavelengths have zero path difference at \(O\)
Refractive index of air is zero
cards.why: At \(O\), \(S_2O = S_1O\) for every wavelength, so all colors interfere constructively.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the central fringe at the mirror contact point in Lloyd's mirror?
options: Dark due to a \(\pi\) phase shift
Bright due to zero path difference
cards.why: Reflection at the denser mirror introduces an abrupt phase shift of \(\pi\), making the contact point dark.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A sheet with \(n = 1.5\) shifts fringes by \(5\lambda\) for \(\lambda = 0.5\,\mu\text{m}\). Find \(t\) in \(\mu\text{m}\).
cards.why: From \((n - 1)t = 5\lambda\), \(0.5t = 2.5\,\mu\text{m}\), so \(t = 5\,\mu\text{m}\).

cards.title: Splitting one wave at the top and bottom of a thin film
cards.meaning: Division of amplitude splits an incoming wave into two reflections — one from the top surface of a thin film and one from the bottom surface — that then interfere.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="24" y="92" width="212" height="52" class="s ok"/><line x1="34" y1="24" x2="82" y2="92" class="ik"/><line x1="82" y1="92" x2="138" y2="20" class="lk"/><line x1="82" y1="92" x2="114" y2="144" class="lk"/><line x1="114" y1="144" x2="146" y2="92" class="lk"/><line x1="146" y1="92" x2="202" y2="20" class="ik"/><line x1="146" y1="92" x2="112" y2="65" class="gk"/><text x="42" y="84" class="t">n₁ (air)</text><text x="42" y="122" class="t">n₂, d</text><text x="80" y="104" class="t">B</text><text x="110" y="158" class="t">D</text><text x="150" y="104" class="t">F</text><text x="102" y="58" class="t">C</text><text x="176" y="122" class="t">Δ = 2n₂d cos θ'</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at incident ray hitting B: the upper reflection and the lower reflection (via B–D–F) travel side by side with optical path difference Δ = 2n₂d cos θ'.
cards.example: At normal incidence (θ' = 0, cos θ' = 1) on a film in air, the extra optical path is 2nd and the upper reflection shifts phase by π.
cards.bridge: When the film index lies between the two surrounding media (like oil on flint glass or MgF₂ on glass), both reflections shift phase by π.

cards.label: 01 · §§15.1–15.3 Definition
cards.title: What is division of amplitude and the cosine law?
cards.body: In division of amplitude at a plane parallel film of thickness d and index n₂, the lower reflection travels an extra optical path Δ = 2n₂d cos θ' given by the cosine law.
cards.tex: \Delta = 2n_2 d\cos\theta' = m\lambda \;(\text{minima in air}), \quad \left(m + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\lambda \;(\text{maxima in air})
examples: Film in air: π shift at top
n₁ < n₂ < n₃: π at both

cards.label: 02 · §15.3 Derivation
cards.title: The cosine law for a plane parallel thin film
cards.legend: Film of thickness \(d\) and index \(n_2\) in medium \(n_1\), incidence angle \(\theta\), refraction angle \(\theta'\), image point \(B'\) at depth \(2d\) (Eqs. 15.3–15.9, Fig. 15.5).

phases.name: Optical path
phases.why: write extra optical path Δ = n₂(BD + DF) - n₁ BC

phases.name: Image point B'
phases.why: extend BJ = JB' = d so BD + DF = B'F

phases.name: Snell's law
phases.why: express n₁ BC as n₂ KF using Snell's law

phases.name: Cosine law
phases.why: replace B'F - KF with B'K = 2d cos θ'

steps.note: Start with the optical path difference between the lower and upper reflections (Eq. 15.3).
Reflect \(B\) across the lower surface to \(B'\) so \(BD = B'D\) and \(BD + DF = B'F\) (Eq. 15.7).

ask.q: Since \(BJ = JB' = d\), why does \(BD + DF\) equal \(B'F\)?
ask.why: Right triangles \(BDJ\) and \(B'DJ\) give \(BD = B'D\), so \(B'D + DF = B'F\).

steps.note: Since \(BC = BF\sin\theta\) and \(KF = BF\sin\theta'\), Snell's law gives \(n_1 BC = n_2 KF\) (Eq. 15.8).

ask.q: Using \(BC = BF\sin\theta\) and \(KF = BF\sin\theta'\), what does \(n_1 BC\) equal?
ask.why: By Snell's law \(n_1\sin\theta = n_2\sin\theta'\), so \(n_1 BC = n_1 BF\sin\theta = n_2 BF\sin\theta' = n_2 KF\).

steps.note: Factor out \(n_2\) on the right-hand side.
Since \(K\) lies on segment \(B'F\), \(B'F - KF = B'K\).

ask.q: Along straight line \(B'KF\), what segment equals \(B'F - KF\)?
ask.why: Point \(K\) divides \(B'F\) into \(B'K\) and \(KF\), so \(B'F - KF = B'K\).

steps.note: In right triangle \(BB'K\) with \(BB' = 2d\), \(B'K = 2d\cos\theta'\) (Eq. 15.9, the cosine law).

ask.q: In right triangle \(BB'K\) with hypotenuse \(BB' = 2d\), what is \(B'K\)?
ask.why: Side \(B'K\) is adjacent to angle \(\angle BB'K = \theta'\) and hypotenuse \(BB' = 2d\).

cards.title: Making glass invisible by cancelling its own reflection
cards.meaning: A non-reflecting film is a quarter-wavelength coating on glass whose top and bottom reflections are equal in strength and opposite in phase, so they cancel out.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="24" y="72" width="212" height="42" class="s ok"/><rect x="24" y="114" width="212" height="46" class="s ok"/><line x1="56" y1="18" x2="76" y2="72" class="ik"/><line x1="76" y1="72" x2="98" y2="18" class="lk"/><line x1="76" y1="72" x2="96" y2="114" class="lk"/><line x1="96" y1="114" x2="116" y2="72" class="lk"/><line x1="116" y1="72" x2="138" y2="18" class="ik"/><text x="184" y="58" class="t">Air (n_a = 1)</text><text x="184" y="96" class="t">Film (n_f < n_g)</text><text x="184" y="140" class="t">Glass (n_g)</text><text x="46" y="34" class="t">(1)</text><text x="94" y="34" class="t">(2)</text><text x="142" y="34" class="t">(5)</text><text x="28" y="96" class="t">d = λ/(4n_f)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at reflected rays (2) and (5): both reflect off denser media (π shift each), and the extra path 2n_f d = λ/2 puts them out of phase.
cards.example: Uncoated crown glass (n = 1.5) reflects 4% at each surface; a λ/(4n_f) MgF₂ film (n_f = 1.38) cuts reflection to 1.3% (blooming).
cards.bridge: Complete cancellation occurs when 2n_f d = λ/2 (so d = λ/(4n_f)) and the two reflected amplitudes match, giving n_f = √(n_a n_g).

cards.label: 03 · §15.4 Definition
cards.title: What is a non-reflecting film (blooming)?
cards.body: A non-reflecting film is a dielectric layer of index n_f between air (n_a) and glass (n_g) and thickness d = λ/(4n_f) that cancels reflected waves by destructive interference.

cards.label: 04 · §15.4 Derivation
cards.title: Thickness and refractive index of a non-reflecting film
cards.legend: Air index \(n_a\), film index \(n_f\), glass index \(n_g\) with \(n_a < n_f < n_g\) at near-normal incidence (Eqs. 15.15–15.18, Fig. 15.7).

phases.name: Destructive phase
phases.why: equate round-trip optical path 2n_f d to half a wavelength

phases.name: Quarter-wave
phases.why: divide by 2n_f to find minimum film thickness d

phases.name: Equal amplitudes
phases.why: equate upper and lower reflected amplitudes for complete cancellation

phases.name: Optimal index
phases.why: cross-multiply and solve for n_f

steps.note: Since \(n_a < n_f < n_g\), both reflections shift phase by \(\pi\), so destructive interference requires \(2n_f d = \lambda/2\).
Divide by \(2n_f\) to get the quarter-wave film thickness (Eq. 15.15).

ask.q: Why does destructive interference occur at \(2n_f d = \lambda/2\) instead of \(\lambda\)?
options: Both interfaces suffer a \(\pi\) phase shift
Neither interface has a phase shift
Only the glass interface shifts phase
Light speeds up inside the film
ask.why: Because \(n_a < n_f < n_g\), both reflections are at denser media and their \(\pi\) shifts cancel.

move.label: Equate reflected amplitudes of rays (2) and (5) (Eq. 15.17)

steps.note: For complete cancellation (with \(4n_a n_f/(n_f+n_a)^2 \approx 1\)), equate the two Fresnel reflection coefficients (Eq. 15.17).

ask.q: For complete destructive interference, what must be true of rays (2) and (5)?
ask.why: Two out-of-phase waves cancel completely only when their amplitudes are equal.

steps.note: Cross-multiply by \((n_f + n_a)(n_g + n_f)\).

steps.tex: n_f^2 - n_a n_g = n_a n_g - n_f^2
steps.note: Expand both sides and cancel \(n_f n_g - n_a n_f\).

ask.q: When both products are expanded, which terms cancel from both sides?
ask.why: Both sides contain \(+n_f n_g - n_a n_f\), leaving \(n_f^2 - n_a n_g = n_a n_g - n_f^2\).

steps.note: Collect \(2n_f^2 = 2n_a n_g\) and divide by 2.
Take the square root to obtain the ideal anti-reflective film index (Eq. 15.18).

ask.q: For crown glass (\(n_g = 1.5\)) in air (\(n_a = 1\)), what is the ideal \(n_f\)?

cards.label: 05 · §15.4.2 Graph
cards.title: Reflectivity R(δ) of an anti-reflecting film (Fig. 15.9)
cards.body: For n_a = 1, n_g = 1.5, and n_f = √1.5 ≈ 1.225, reflectivity R drops to zero at δ = π/2, 3π/2, 5π/2 (d = λ/4n_f, 3λ/4n_f). A λ/4n_f film is used because R(λ) stays lowest across visible wavelengths.

cards.label: 06 · §15.4 Worked calculation
cards.title: MgF₂ non-reflecting coating thickness & reflectivity (§15.4)
cards.tex: d = \frac{5.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}}{4 \times 1.38} \approx 0.9 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}, \quad R = \left(\frac{n_a n_g - n_f^2}{n_a n_g + n_f^2}\right)^2 \approx 1.3\%
cards.body: For \(\lambda = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}\) and \(\text{MgF}_2\) (\(n_f = 1.38\)) on crown glass (\(n_g = 1.5\)), thickness is \(d \approx 0.9 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}\) and reflectivity drops from \(4\%\) to \(1.3\%\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: For a film of index \(n_2 = 1.60\) between crown glass (1.52) and flint glass (1.66) at normal incidence, when do maxima occur?
cards.why: Since \(1.52 < 1.60 < 1.66\), a \(\pi\) phase shift occurs at both interfaces, so \(2nd = m\lambda\) gives maxima (Eq. 15.2b).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Reducing lens surface reflectivity with a thin quarter-wave coating is called ______.
cards.why: Coating a lens with a \(\lambda/(4n_f)\) film to reduce reflection losses is known as blooming (§15.4).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Find the minimum non-reflecting thickness \(d\) in nm for \(\lambda = 552\text{ nm}\) and \(n_f = 1.38\).

cards.title: Contour lines of constant thickness on a soap film or wedge
cards.meaning: Fringes of equal thickness are bright and dark bands that trace out places where a thin film has the exact same thickness.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="24,132 232,132 232,76" class="s ok"/><line x1="24" y1="132" x2="236" y2="132" class="ik"/><line x1="24" y1="132" x2="232" y2="76" class="lk"/><line x1="76" y1="28" x2="76" y2="132" class="gk"/><line x1="128" y1="28" x2="128" y2="132" class="gk"/><line x1="180" y1="28" x2="180" y2="132" class="gk"/><circle cx="76" cy="118" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="128" cy="104" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="180" cy="90" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="76" y="22" text-anchor="middle" class="t">t = λ/2</text><text x="128" y="22" text-anchor="middle" class="t">t = λ</text><text x="180" y="22" text-anchor="middle" class="t">t = 3λ/2</text><text x="130" y="156" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Each fringe = locus of constant thickness t</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the thin wedge film: each vertical line marks a thickness t = mλ/2 where a dark fringe forms.
cards.example: When sunlight hits a soap bubble or oil film on water, different colors constructively interfere at different thicknesses, painting colored contour bands.
cards.bridge: If the film is thicker than a few wavelengths, many colors overlap at every point and the white-light fringes wash out.

cards.label: 01 · §15.9 Definition
cards.title: What are fringes of equal thickness and thin-film colors?
cards.body: In a thin film of varying thickness illuminated by an extended source, each fringe follows a locus of constant film thickness; white light produces colored fringes if the film is very thin.

objects.text: Constant thickness t along each fringe
objects.name: film

cards.title: Circular air-film fringes under a curved lens
cards.meaning: Newton's rings are concentric dark and bright circles formed because the air gap between a spherical lens and a flat glass plate has constant thickness around each circle.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M 22 48 Q 92 128 162 48 Z" class="s ok"/><line x1="18" y1="88" x2="166" y2="88" class="ik"/><line x1="92" y1="22" x2="92" y2="88" class="gk"/><line x1="132" y1="72" x2="132" y2="88" class="lk"/><circle cx="92" cy="88" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="212" cy="88" r="6" class="f"/><circle cx="212" cy="88" r="16" class="lk"/><circle cx="212" cy="88" r="24" class="ik"/><circle cx="212" cy="88" r="31" class="lk"/><circle cx="212" cy="88" r="37" class="ik"/><text x="92" y="104" text-anchor="middle" class="t">O (t=0)</text><text x="112" y="104" text-anchor="middle" class="t">r_m</text><text x="142" y="82" class="t">t</text><text x="78" y="34" class="t">R</text><text x="212" y="144" text-anchor="middle" class="t">r_m = √(mλR)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the lens touching the flat plate at O (left) and the concentric rings getting closer together outward (right).
cards.example: At the contact point O, thickness t = 0, so the π phase shift at the lower glass plate makes the central spot dark.
cards.bridge: From circle geometry r_m² = t(2R - t) ≈ 2Rt and the dark-ring condition 2t = mλ, the m-th dark ring has radius r_m = √(mλR).

cards.label: 02 · §15.10 Definition
cards.title: What are Newton's rings?
cards.body: Newton's rings are concentric dark and bright circular fringes formed by interference in the thin air film between a plano-convex lens of radius R and a plane glass plate.

cards.label: 03 · §15.10 Derivation
cards.title: Radii of dark rings and wavelength in Newton's rings
cards.legend: Lens of radius of curvature \(R\) on flat glass plate \(POQ\), air-film thickness \(t\) at dark ring radius \(r_m\) and diameter \(D_m = 2r_m\) (Eqs. 15.63–15.68, Fig. 15.30).

phases.name: Circle geometry
phases.why: relate ring radius r_m to film thickness t and lens radius R

phases.name: Thin air film
phases.why: neglect t compared to 2R since t ≪ R

phases.name: Dark ring radius
phases.why: substitute the dark-ring condition 2t = mλ

phases.name: Ring diameters
phases.why: write λ in terms of diameters D_{m+p} and D_m

steps.note: From the intersecting-chords relation (or right triangle \(R^2 = r_m^2 + (R - t)^2\)), \(r_m^2 = t(2R - t)\) (Eq. 15.64).

move.label: Neglect t compared to 2R for t ≪ R

steps.note: Since \(R \approx 100\text{ cm}\) and \(t \lesssim 10^{-3}\text{ cm}\), neglect \(t\) compared to \(2R\).

ask.q: Why can \(t\) be neglected inside \((2R - t)\)?
ask.why: The air film thickness \(t \lesssim 10^{-3}\text{ cm}\) is tiny compared to \(R \approx 100\text{ cm}\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(R\) to isolate \(2t\) (Eq. 15.65).
Substitute the air-film dark-ring condition \(2t = m\lambda\) (Eq. 15.63).

ask.q: For the \(m\)-th dark ring in an air film (\(n = 1\)), what is \(2t\)?
ask.why: With the \(\pi\) phase shift at the lower plate, destructive interference occurs at \(2t = m\lambda\).

steps.note: Multiply by \(R\); thus dark ring radii vary as \(\sqrt{m}\) (Eq. 15.66).

ask.q: How do the radii \(r_m\) of dark Newton's rings scale with order \(m\)?
ask.why: Since \(r_m = \sqrt{m\lambda R}\), radii grow as the square root of natural numbers \(m\).

steps.note: With diameter \(D_m = 2r_m\), \(D_{m+p}^2 - D_m^2 = 4[(m+p)\lambda R - m\lambda R] = 4p\lambda R\).
Divide both sides by \(4pR\).
Swap sides to get the wavelength formula from two ring diameters (Eq. 15.68).

ask.q: Why do we measure \(D_{m+p}^2 - D_m^2\) instead of a single diameter \(D_m^2\)?
options: Dust or imperfect contact cancels out
It makes the rings equally spaced
ask.why: Any constant gap offset at \(O\) due to dust cancels when \(r_m^2\) is subtracted from \(r_{m+p}^2\).

cards.title: Two perpendicular mirror arms acting like a tunable air film
cards.meaning: The Michelson interferometer splits a light beam at 45° toward two perpendicular mirrors M₁ and M₂, creating an equivalent air film between M₁ and the virtual image M₂'.
cards.picture: Look at beam splitter G₁, compensating plate G₂, movable mirror M₁, and virtual image M₂' separated by d = x₁ ~ x₂.
cards.example: As mirror M₁ moves toward M₂' reducing d, circular fringes collapse into the center; N collapsed fringes over distance d₀ give λ = 2d₀/N.
cards.bridge: Compensating plate G₂ equalizes the glass path in both arms so white-light fringes can be seen at d = 0.

cards.label: 04 · §15.11 Definition
cards.title: What is the Michelson interferometer?
cards.body: The Michelson interferometer uses a 45° beam splitter G₁, compensating plate G₂, and perpendicular mirrors M₁ and M₂ to form circular fringes of equal inclination with path difference 2d cos θ.

cards.label: 05 · §§15.10–15.11 Examples
cards.title: Lifting the lens & sodium doublet Δλ (Examples 15.2, 15.4)
cards.body: Raising the Newton's-rings lens or moving \(M_1\) toward \(M_2'\) causes rings to collapse to the center. For sodium (\(\lambda = 5890\text{ \AA}\)), successive disappearances every \(\Delta d = 0.289\text{ mm}\) give \(\Delta\lambda = (5890\text{ \AA})^2 / 0.578\text{ mm} \approx 6\text{ \AA}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What happens to Newton's rings when the convex lens is slowly raised above the plate?
options: The rings collapse toward the center
The rings turn into straight lines
cards.why: Increasing the central gap means a given thickness \(t = m\lambda/2\) occurs at a smaller radius, so rings collapse inward (Example 15.2).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Why is a compensating plate \(G_2\) needed in a Michelson interferometer?
options: To equalize glass paths for white light
To focus circular rings without a lens
cards.why: Because refractive index varies with wavelength (dispersion), \(G_2\) ensures both beams traverse the glass plate three times for white light (§15.11).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: In a Michelson interferometer, 1000 fringes collapse when \(M_1\) moves \(0.29\text{ mm}\). Find \(\lambda\) in nm.
cards.why: \(\lambda = \frac{2d_0}{N} = \frac{2 \times 0.29 \times 10^6\text{ nm}}{1000} = 580\text{ nm}\).

cards.title: Moving the source and screen to infinity with two lenses
cards.meaning: Fraunhofer diffraction happens when the incoming wave and the outgoing diffracted waves are flat plane waves, which we easily get by using two convex lenses.
cards.picture: Look at the two lenses: the first turns light from S into a parallel beam on slit b, and lens L focuses parallel rays at angle θ to point P.
cards.example: In a school laboratory spectrometer, the collimator provides parallel rays and the telescope focuses them onto the crosswires.
cards.bridge: Inside the slit of width b, we model the plane wavefront as n equally spaced Huygens point sources A₁, A₂, …, A_n with spacing Δ so b = (n - 1)Δ.

cards.label: 01 · §§18.1–18.2 Definition
cards.title: What is Fraunhofer diffraction at a single slit?
cards.body: Fraunhofer diffraction occurs when source and screen are effectively at infinity using lenses. A plane wave hitting a slit of width b excites n point sources of spacing Δ that send parallel rays at angle θ to P.

cards.label: 02 · §18.2 Derivation
cards.title: Single-slit Fraunhofer amplitude and intensity
cards.legend: Slit of width \(b = (n-1)\Delta\) with \(n\) Huygens point sources \(A_1, A_2, \dots\), diffraction angle \(\theta\), and \(\beta = \frac{\pi b\sin\theta}{\lambda}\) (Eqs. 18.1–18.10, Fig. 18.3).

phases.name: Phase step
phases.why: write phase lag φ between adjacent point sources separated by Δ

phases.name: Sum wavelets
phases.why: add the n cosine waves and sum the trigonometric series

phases.name: Continuous limit
phases.why: let n → ∞ and Δ → 0 with nΔ → b so nφ/2 → β

phases.name: Intensity law
phases.why: square the field amplitude to obtain the sinc-squared intensity

steps.note: Adjacent sources \(A_1, A_2\) at spacing \(\Delta\) have path difference \(\Delta\sin\theta\) (Eq. 18.2).

move.label: Superpose the n secondary wavelets at P (Eq. 18.3)

steps.note: Each point source sends a wave of amplitude \(a\) shifted in phase by \(\phi\) from its neighbour (Eq. 18.3).

ask.q: What is the amplitude \(E_\theta\) of this sum of \(n\) cosine terms?
ask.why: Summing \(n\) harmonic waves with uniform phase step \(\phi\) gives amplitude \(a\frac{\sin(n\phi/2)}{\sin(\phi/2)}\) (Eq. 18.6).

steps.note: Write the resultant amplitude \(E_\theta\) of the \(n\) interfering point sources (Eq. 18.6).
In the continuous limit \(n \to \infty, \Delta \to 0\) with \(n\Delta \to b\), \(n\phi/2\) becomes \((\pi b\sin\theta)/\lambda\).

ask.q: As \(n \to \infty\) and \(\Delta \to 0\), what does the product \(n\Delta\) approach?
ask.why: Since \(b = (n - 1)\Delta\), letting \(n \to \infty\) and \(\Delta \to 0\) makes \(n\Delta\) approach the total slit width \(b\).

steps.note: Define the dimensionless diffraction variable \(\beta\) as half the phase difference across the whole slit (Eq. 18.8).

ask.q: Since \(\phi/2 = \beta/n\) is very small as \(n \to \infty\), what replaces \(\sin(\phi/2)\)?
ask.why: For an infinitesimally small angle \(\phi/2 = \beta/n\), \(\sin(\phi/2) \approx \phi/2 = \beta/n\).

steps.note: Replace \(\sin(\phi/2)\) by \(\beta/n\) and set \(A = na\) for the central amplitude at \(\theta = 0\) (Eq. 18.7).

move.label: Include the harmonic time factor cos(ωt - β) (Eq. 18.9)

steps.note: Since \(\frac{1}{2}(n-1)\phi \to \beta\), the resultant electric field at \(P\) is Eq. (18.9).

ask.q: Since intensity \(I\) is proportional to \(E_\theta^2\), how does \(I\) depend on \(\beta\)?
ask.why: Squaring the amplitude \(E_\theta = A(\sin\beta/\beta)\) gives \(I = I_0(\sin^2\beta/\beta^2)\) (Eq. 18.10).

move.label: Square the amplitude and set I₀ ∝ A² (Eq. 18.10)

steps.note: This is the single-slit Fraunhofer intensity distribution, where \(I_0\) is the intensity at \(\theta = 0\) (Eq. 18.10).

cards.title: Why the top and bottom halves of a slit cancel at the first dark band
cards.meaning: At the first dark minimum (b sin θ = λ), we can pair every point in the upper half of the slit with a twin point b/2 below it that is half a wavelength out of step.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="64" y1="14" x2="64" y2="40" class="ik"/><line x1="64" y1="144" x2="64" y2="170" class="ik"/><line x1="64" y1="92" x2="54" y2="92" class="gk"/><line x1="64" y1="46" x2="196" y2="22" class="lk"/><line x1="64" y1="66" x2="196" y2="42" class="ik"/><line x1="64" y1="98" x2="196" y2="74" class="lk"/><line x1="64" y1="118" x2="196" y2="94" class="ik"/><line x1="64" y1="46" x2="73" y2="96" class="gk"/><circle cx="64" cy="46" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="64" cy="66" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="64" cy="98" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="64" cy="118" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="48" y="50" class="t">A</text><text x="48" y="70" class="t">B</text><text x="46" y="102" class="t">A'</text><text x="46" y="122" class="t">B'</text><text x="18" y="76" class="t">b/2</text><text x="18" y="118" class="t">b/2</text><text x="152" y="130" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(b/2) sin θ = λ/2 → phase π</text><text x="152" y="152" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Pairs (A, A') and (B, B') cancel!</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at twin points A and A' separated by b/2: when b sin θ = λ, their path difference is λ/2 so they cancel completely.
cards.example: In the same way, when b sin θ = 2λ, dividing the slit into 4 equal quarters makes adjacent quarters cancel in pairs.
cards.bridge: Between the zero-intensity minima at β = mπ (m = ±1, ±2, …), differentiating I(β) gives secondary maxima where tan β = β.

cards.label: 03 · §18.2.1 Definition
cards.title: What is the single-slit diffraction pattern?
cards.body: The single-slit pattern has a central maximum I = I₀ at θ = 0 (since sin β/β → 1), dark minima I = 0 at b sin θ = mλ (m = ±1, ±2, …), and weak secondary maxima at the roots of tan β = β.

cards.label: 04 · §18.2.1 Intensity graph
cards.title: Single-slit intensity distribution I = I₀(sin²β/β²) (Fig. 18.4)
cards.body: The central maximum at β = 0 reaches I₀, flanked by zero minima at β = ±π, ±2π, ±3π. Secondary maxima at roots of tan β = β (β = ±1.43π, ±2.46π) have heights 4.96% and 1.68% of I₀.

cards.label: 05 · §18.2.1 Examples 18.1–18.2
cards.title: Worked example: minima spacing and central maximum width
cards.tex: \theta_1 \approx \frac{\lambda}{b} = \frac{5\times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}}{2\times 10^{-2}\text{ cm}} = 2.5\times 10^{-3}\text{ rad}, \quad W = 2\theta_1 D = 1.5\text{ cm}
cards.body: For \(b = 0.2\text{ mm}\) and \(\lambda = 5\times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}\), first and second minima are at \(2.5\times 10^{-3}\) and \(5\times 10^{-3}\text{ rad}\), separated by \(0.05\text{ cm}\) on a focal plane with \(f = 20\text{ cm}\). At screen distance \(D = 3\text{ m}\), total central width is \(2\theta_1 D = 1.5\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Where do zero-intensity minima occur in single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction?
cards.why: Intensity \(I = I_0(\sin^2\beta/\beta^2)\) vanishes when \(\beta = m\pi\) with \(m \neq 0\), giving \(b\sin\theta = m\lambda\) (Eq. 18.12).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Which equation gives the positions of single-slit secondary maxima?
cards.why: Setting \(dI/d\beta = 0\) yields \(\sin\beta(\beta - \tan\beta) = 0\), so maxima satisfy \(\tan\beta = \beta\) (Eq. 18.16).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: At the first minimum \(b\sin\theta = \lambda\), the two equal ______ of the slit cancel each other.
cards.why: Dividing the slit into two halves of width \(b/2\) pairs every point \(A\) with a point \(A'\) having path difference \(\lambda/2\) (Fig. 18.5).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A slit of width \(b = 0.1\text{ mm}\) is lit by \(\lambda = 500\text{ nm}\). Find first minimum angle \(\theta_1\) in mrad.
cards.why: \(\theta_1 \approx \frac{\lambda}{b} = \frac{5\times 10^{-7}\text{ m}}{10^{-4}\text{ m}} = 5\times 10^{-3}\text{ rad} = 5\text{ mrad}\).

cards.title: Interference fringes tucked inside a diffraction envelope
cards.meaning: When two slits each have width b and center-to-center distance d, each slit creates a wide diffraction envelope while the two slits interfere to carve narrow fringes inside it.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="46" y1="16" x2="46" y2="48" class="ik"/><line x1="46" y1="68" x2="46" y2="112" class="ik"/><line x1="46" y1="132" x2="46" y2="164" class="ik"/><path d="M 134 26 Q 122 90 134 154 Q 146 90 134 26 Z" class="s ok"/><line x1="216" y1="18" x2="216" y2="162" class="ik"/><line x1="46" y1="58" x2="134" y2="44" class="lk"/><line x1="46" y1="122" x2="134" y2="108" class="lk"/><line x1="134" y1="44" x2="216" y2="52" class="lk"/><line x1="134" y1="108" x2="216" y2="52" class="lk"/><line x1="46" y1="58" x2="54" y2="120" class="gk"/><circle cx="46" cy="58" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="46" cy="122" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="216" cy="52" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="216" cy="90" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="26" y="62" class="t">b</text><text x="26" y="94" class="t">d</text><text x="26" y="126" class="t">b</text><text x="82" y="138" class="t">d sin θ</text><text x="176" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">f</text><text x="226" y="56" class="t">P</text><text x="226" y="94" class="t">O</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the two slits of width b separated by distance d: corresponding points (A₁, B₁) have path difference d sin θ to point P.
cards.example: If the slits become very narrow (b → 0 so sin β / β ≈ 1), the diffraction factor stays near 1 and we recover Young's cos²γ interference fringes.
cards.bridge: Adding the fields E₁ and E₂ from the two slits gives intensity I = 4I₀(sin²β / β²) cos²γ, the product of diffraction and interference factors.

cards.label: 01 · §18.6 Definition
cards.title: What is the two-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern?
cards.body: The two-slit Fraunhofer pattern of two parallel slits (width b, separation d) has intensity equal to the product of the single-slit diffraction factor (sin²β/β²) and the two-source interference factor (cos²γ).

cards.label: 02 · §18.6 Derivation
cards.title: Two-slit Fraunhofer field and intensity distribution
cards.legend: Two slits of width \(b\) separated by distance \(d\), phase lag \(\Phi_1 = 2\gamma = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}d\sin\theta\) between corresponding points \((A_1, B_1)\) (Eqs. 18.44–18.45, Fig. 18.29).

phases.name: Slit fields
phases.why: write the diffracted field E₁ from the first slit of width b

phases.name: Phase lag
phases.why: find phase difference Φ₁ between corresponding points separated by d

phases.name: Superpose
phases.why: add E₁ + E₂ and factor with the cosine sum identity

phases.name: Product law
phases.why: define γ = Φ₁/2 and square the amplitude to get intensity

steps.note: The first slit of width \(b\) produces the single-slit field \(E_1\) at point \(P\) (Eq. 18.9).

move.label: Write phase lag Φ₁ between corresponding points (A₁, B₁)

steps.note: Corresponding points \((A_1, B_1)\) are separated by \(d\), giving path difference \(d\sin\theta\) and phase lag \(\Phi_1\).

ask.q: With phase lag \(\Phi_1\), what is the field \(E_2\) from the second slit?
ask.why: The second slit has the same width \(b\) (same amplitude \(A\sin\beta/\beta\)) delayed in phase by \(\Phi_1\).

move.label: Add fields E₁ and E₂ at screen point P

steps.note: Superpose \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) and factor out the common single-slit amplitude \(A(\sin\beta/\beta)\).

ask.q: What does \(\cos C + \cos D\) equal by trigonometry?
ask.why: By the sum-to-product identity, \(\cos C + \cos D = 2\cos\frac{C-D}{2}\cos\frac{C+D}{2}\).

steps.note: Combine the two cosines using half the phase difference \(\Phi_1 / 2\).
Define the interference phase parameter \(\gamma = \Phi_1 / 2\) (Eq. 18.44).

ask.q: What is the ratio \(\gamma / \beta\) for slit separation \(d\) and width \(b\)?
ask.why: Since \(\gamma = (\pi d\sin\theta)/\lambda\) and \(\beta = (\pi b\sin\theta)/\lambda\), their ratio is \(\gamma/\beta = d/b\).

steps.note: Substitute \(\gamma = \Phi_1 / 2\) into the resultant electric field.

ask.q: When we square the amplitude \(2A(\sin\beta/\beta)\cos\gamma\), what is the intensity \(I\)?
ask.why: Since \(I_0\) corresponds to \(A^2\), squaring the amplitude gives \(I = 4I_0(\sin^2\beta/\beta^2)\cos^2\gamma\) (Eq. 18.45).

move.label: Square the amplitude and set I₀ ∝ A² (Eq. 18.45)

steps.note: The resultant intensity is the product of the single-slit diffraction pattern and two-slit interference pattern (Eq. 18.45).

cards.title: When a bright interference fringe lands on a dark diffraction zero
cards.meaning: A missing order happens when the two slits try to make a bright interference peak at the exact angle where each individual slit sends zero light.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="18" y1="144" x2="242" y2="144" class="lk"/><line x1="130" y1="22" x2="130" y2="156" class="gk"/><path d="M 34 144 Q 56 130 74 144 Q 102 22 130 22 Q 158 22 186 144 Q 204 130 226 144" class="gk"/><polyline points="74,144 81,126 88,144 95,88 102,144 109,46 116,144 123,25 130,22 137,25 144,144 151,46 158,144 165,88 172,144 179,126 186,144" class="lk"/><circle cx="74" cy="144" r="8" class="s ok"/><circle cx="186" cy="144" r="8" class="s ok"/><text x="74" y="164" text-anchor="middle" class="t">-π (missing)</text><text x="186" y="164" text-anchor="middle" class="t">+π (missing)</text><text x="130" y="16" text-anchor="middle" class="t">d = 4b → 4th order missing at β = ±π</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the two small circles at β = ±π: the dashed diffraction envelope touches zero right where the 4th interference peak would sit.
cards.example: Because 0 × 1 = 0, the zero of sin²β / β² wipes out the interference peak where cos²γ = 1.
cards.bridge: Mathematically, missing orders occur when d sin θ = nλ and b sin θ = mλ hold together, so n / m = d / b.

cards.label: 03 · §18.6.1 Definition
cards.title: What are maxima, minima, and missing orders in two-slit diffraction?
cards.body: Diffraction minima occur at b sin θ = mλ (m = 1, 2, …) and interference minima at d sin θ = (n + ½)λ. Missing orders occur when an interference maximum d sin θ = nλ coincides with a diffraction minimum b sin θ = mλ.

objects.text: Missing order at sin θ = mλ/b = nλ/d
objects.name: env

cards.label: 04 · §18.6.1 Intensity graph
cards.title: Double-slit intensity distribution with missing order (Fig. 18.31)
cards.body: For d = 4b, rapid cos²(4β) interference fringes sit inside the sin²β/β² diffraction envelope. The n = ±4 interference maxima fall on the m = ±1 diffraction minima at β = ±π and are missing (circled).

cards.label: 05 · §18.6.1 Example 18.9
cards.title: Worked example: interference minima and fringe width
cards.body: For \(b = 8.8\times 10^{-3}\text{ cm}\), \(d = 7.0\times 10^{-2}\text{ cm}\), and \(\lambda = 6.328\times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}\), the first diffraction minimum is at \(\sin\theta = \lambda/b = 7.19\times 10^{-3}\) (\(0.412^\circ\)), enclosing 8 interference minima on each side (16 total). At \(D = 15\text{ ft}\), fringe width is \(0.0413\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In \(I = 4I_0(\sin^2\beta/\beta^2)\cos^2\gamma\), what does \(\cos^2\gamma\) represent?
cards.why: The factor \(\cos^2\gamma\) is the interference pattern of two point sources separated by \(d\), while \(\sin^2\beta/\beta^2\) is the single-slit diffraction factor (§18.6).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Which condition gives the interference minima in a two-slit pattern?
cards.why: The interference factor \(\cos^2\gamma\) vanishes when \(\gamma = (n + 1/2)\pi\), which gives \(d\sin\theta = (n + 1/2)\lambda\) (Eq. 18.46).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: In a double slit with \(d = 3b\), which positive interference order \(n\) is the first missing order?
cards.why: From \(n/m = d/b = 3\), the first diffraction minimum (\(m = 1\)) eliminates the \(n = 3\) interference maximum.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: If \(d = 4b\), how many bright interference maxima appear strictly inside the central diffraction envelope?
cards.why: Orders \(n = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3\) lie inside \(|\sin\theta| < \lambda/b\), while \(n = \pm 4\) fall on the first diffraction zero, giving \(2(4) - 1 = 7\) bright fringes.

cards.title: Why adding more slits makes the bright peaks needle-sharp
cards.meaning: When N slits send waves in step (d sin θ = mλ), all N amplitudes add to N times a single slit, while just off that angle the N waves cancel at N - 1 dark minima.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="18" y1="146" x2="242" y2="146" class="lk"/><polyline points="30,146 42,24 54,146 66,138 78,146 90,140 102,146 114,138 126,146 138,24 150,146 162,138 174,146 186,140 198,146 210,138 222,146 234,24" class="lk"/><circle cx="42" cy="24" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="138" cy="24" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="234" cy="24" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="42" y="162" text-anchor="middle" class="t">-π</text><text x="138" y="162" text-anchor="middle" class="t">0</text><text x="234" y="162" text-anchor="middle" class="t">+π</text><text x="138" y="18" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Principal maxima: height N²</text><text x="90" y="124" text-anchor="middle" class="t">N - 1 minima</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the tall principal maxima of height N² at γ = -π, 0, +π separated by N - 1 zero secondary minima.
cards.example: With N = 5 slits, the peak height is N² = 25 and the first minimum sits only Δγ = π/5 away from the peak.
cards.bridge: Summing N slit fields gives intensity I = I₀(sin²β / β²)(sin²Nγ / sin²γ), where sin Nγ / sin γ → ±N as γ → mπ.

cards.label: 01 · §18.7 Definition
cards.title: What are principal maxima and secondary minima in N-slit diffraction?
cards.body: For N slits of width b and spacing d, principal maxima occur at γ = mπ (d sin θ = mλ) with intensity N²I₀(sin²β/β²). Between adjacent principal maxima lie (N - 1) secondary minima and (N - 2) weak secondary maxima.

cards.label: 02 · §§18.7.1–18.7.2 Derivation
cards.title: N-slit intensity, principal maxima, and angular half-width
cards.legend: \(N\) parallel slits of width \(b\) and spacing \(d\), \(\gamma = \frac{\pi}{\lambda}d\sin\theta\), \(m\)-th principal maximum at \(\theta_m\) with half-width \(\Delta\theta_m\) (Eqs. 18.48–18.63, Fig. 18.32).

phases.name: Sum N slits
phases.why: add the N slit fields and sum the cosine progression

phases.name: Principal maxima
phases.why: take the limit γ → mπ using L'Hôpital's rule to find peak intensity

phases.name: Adjacent minimum
phases.why: write the condition for the first minimum at θ_m ± Δθ_m

phases.name: Angular half-width
phases.why: expand sin(θ_m ± Δθ_m) for small Δθ_m and solve for Δθ_m

steps.note: Sum the diffracted fields from all \(N\) parallel slits at screen point \(P\) (Eq. 18.48).
With \(\gamma = \Phi_1 / 2 = (\pi d\sin\theta)/\lambda\), sum the \(N\) cosines into closed form (Eq. 18.49).

ask.q: When we square the amplitude of Eq. (18.49), what is the intensity \(I\)?
ask.why: Squaring the amplitude gives the product of the single-slit factor \(\sin^2\beta/\beta^2\) and the \(N\)-slit factor \(\sin^2 N\gamma/\sin^2\gamma\) (Eq. 18.50).

move.label: Square the amplitude to obtain intensity I (Eq. 18.50)

steps.note: This reduces to Eq. (18.10) for \(N = 1\) and to Eq. (18.45) for \(N = 2\) (Eq. 18.50).
At \(\gamma = m\pi\) (\(d\sin\theta_m = m\lambda\)), \(\lim_{\gamma\to m\pi}\frac{\sin N\gamma}{\sin\gamma} = \pm N\), so peak intensity scales as \(N^2\) (Eq. 18.53).

ask.q: Why does \(\sin N\gamma / \sin\gamma\) approach \(\pm N\) as \(\gamma \to m\pi\)?
ask.why: Differentiating numerator and denominator gives \(\lim_{\gamma\to m\pi}(N\cos N\gamma / \cos\gamma) = \pm N\) (§18.7.1).

move.label: Write first minimum on either side of m-th principal maximum (Eq. 18.61)

steps.note: The first secondary minimum beside \(d\sin\theta_m = m\lambda\) occurs at path difference \(m\lambda \pm \lambda/N\) (Eq. 18.61).

ask.q: For small half-width \(\Delta\theta_m\), what approximates \(\sin(\theta_m \pm \Delta\theta_m)\)?
ask.why: Using \(\cos\Delta\theta_m \approx 1\) and \(\sin\Delta\theta_m \approx \Delta\theta_m\) gives \(\sin\theta_m \pm \Delta\theta_m\cos\theta_m\) (Eq. 18.62).

steps.note: Substitute the small-angle expansion Eq. (18.62) into Eq. (18.61).
Cancel \(d\sin\theta_m = m\lambda\) from both sides and take the positive sign.

ask.q: How does the angular half-width \(\Delta\theta_m\) change as slit count \(N\) increases?
ask.why: Dividing by \(Nd\cos\theta_m\) gives \(\Delta\theta_m = \lambda/(Nd\cos\theta_m)\), so peaks become sharper as \(N\) grows (Eq. 18.63).

steps.note: Divide by \(Nd\cos\theta_m\) to obtain the angular half-width of the \(m\)-th principal maximum (Eq. 18.63).

cards.label: 03 · §18.7 Interference graph
cards.title: N-slit interference factor sin²(Nγ)/sin²γ for N = 5 (Fig. 18.33)
cards.body: For N = 5 slits, sharp principal maxima of height N² = 25 occur at γ = 0, ±π, ±2π. Between consecutive principal maxima lie N - 1 = 4 secondary minima (at γ = pπ/5) and N - 2 = 3 weak secondary maxima.

cards.title: Splitting white light into a rainbow with thousands of slits
cards.meaning: A diffraction grating has around 15,000 parallel grooves per inch so that each wavelength λ in a beam is sent to its own sharp angle given by d sin θ = mλ.

cards.picture: Look at the grating between lenses L₁ and L₂: m = 0 stays white at θ = 0, while for m ≥ 1 red bends more than violet.
cards.example: Because sin θ = mλ / d cannot exceed 1, the highest visible order is the integer part of d / λ.
cards.bridge: Differentiating the grating equation d sin θ = mλ with respect to λ gives the angular dispersion Δθ / Δλ = m / (d cos θ).

cards.label: 04 · §§18.8–18.8.1 Definition
cards.title: What is a diffraction grating and its angular dispersion?
cards.body: A diffraction grating has N equidistant slits of grating element d. Its principal maxima satisfy d sin θ = mλ (zeroeth order m = 0 is undispersed white), and its angular dispersion is Δθ/Δλ = m/(d cos θ).

cards.title: When two close spectral lines are just resolved (Rayleigh criterion)
cards.meaning: According to Rayleigh's criterion, two nearby wavelengths λ and λ + Δλ are just resolved when the peak of λ + Δλ lands right on the first dark minimum of λ.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="146" x2="240" y2="146" class="lk"/><path d="M 44 146 Q 76 146 108 34 Q 140 146 156 146" class="lk"/><path d="M 108 146 Q 124 146 156 34 Q 188 146 220 146" class="ik"/><line x1="108" y1="34" x2="108" y2="146" class="gk"/><line x1="156" y1="34" x2="156" y2="146" class="gk"/><circle cx="108" cy="34" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="156" cy="34" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="132" cy="55" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="88" y="34" text-anchor="end" class="t">λ (1.0)</text><text x="166" y="34" class="t">λ + Δλ</text><text x="132" y="46" text-anchor="middle" class="t">0.811</text><text x="132" y="164" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Peak of λ + Δλ at 1st minimum of λ → R = mN</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at angle θ under the second peak: it is simultaneously the m-th maximum of λ + Δλ and the first minimum of λ.
cards.example: At the midpoint between the two just-resolved peaks, the combined intensity dips to 0.811 of either peak (Fig. 18.39).
cards.bridge: Equating d sin θ = m(λ + Δλ) and d sin θ = mλ + λ/N immediately gives resolving power R = λ / Δλ = mN.

cards.label: 05 · §18.8.2 Definition
cards.title: What is the resolving power of a diffraction grating?
cards.body: The resolving power R = λ/Δλ of a grating is its power to distinguish two nearby spectral lines λ and λ + Δλ. By the Rayleigh criterion, R equals the product of diffraction order m and total exposed lines N.

objects.text: d sin θ = m(λ+Δλ) = mλ + λ/N
objects.name: common

cards.label: 06 · §§18.8.1–18.8.2 Derivation
cards.title: Grating angular dispersion and resolving power R = mN
cards.legend: Grating element \(d\), spectral order \(m\), total exposed lines \(N\), and just-resolved wavelengths \(\lambda\) and \(\lambda + \Delta\lambda\) at angle \(\theta\) (Eqs. 18.64–18.69, Fig. 18.39).

phases.name: Dispersion
phases.why: differentiate d sin θ = mλ to find angular dispersion Δθ/Δλ

phases.name: Rayleigh match
phases.why: place the m-th peak of λ + Δλ on the first minimum of λ

phases.name: Equate paths
phases.why: equate the two expressions for d sin θ and cancel mλ

phases.name: Resolving power
phases.why: rearrange for R = λ / Δλ = mN

steps.note: Start from the grating equation for the \(m\)-th principal maximum (Eq. 18.64).
Differentiate both sides with respect to \(\lambda\) for a small wavelength interval \(\Delta\lambda\).

ask.q: How do we isolate the angular dispersion \(\Delta\theta / \Delta\lambda\)?
ask.why: Dividing by \(d\cos\theta\) gives \(\Delta\theta/\Delta\lambda = m/(d\cos\theta)\) (Eq. 18.65).

steps.note: Smaller grating element \(d\) and higher order \(m\) give larger angular dispersion (Eq. 18.65).

move.label: Write m-th principal maximum for wavelength λ + Δλ at angle θ (Eq. 18.67)

steps.note: At common angle \(\theta\), wavelength \(\lambda + \Delta\lambda\) forms its \(m\)-th principal maximum (Eq. 18.67).

move.label: Write first minimum of wavelength λ at the same angle θ (Eq. 18.68)

steps.note: At the same angle \(\theta\), wavelength \(\lambda\) has its first adjacent minimum (Eq. 18.68).

ask.q: By the Rayleigh criterion, why are Eqs. (18.67) and (18.68) equal?
options: Both hold at the same angle \(\theta\)
ask.why: The peak of \(\lambda + \Delta\lambda\) and the first minimum of \(\lambda\) occur at the same angle \(\theta\).

steps.note: Equate the right-hand sides of Eqs. (18.67) and (18.68) and expand \(m(\lambda + \Delta\lambda)\).

ask.q: What remains after subtracting \(m\lambda\) from both sides?
ask.why: Subtracting \(m\lambda\) from both sides leaves \(m\Delta\lambda = \lambda / N\).

steps.note: Subtract \(m\lambda\) from both sides.

ask.q: How do we rearrange \(m\Delta\lambda = \lambda / N\) to get \(R = \lambda / \Delta\lambda\)?
ask.why: Multiplying by \(N/\Delta\lambda\) gives \(\lambda / \Delta\lambda = mN\) (Eq. 18.69).

steps.note: Resolving power equals the product of spectral order \(m\) and total illuminated rulings \(N\) (Eq. 18.69).

cards.label: 07 · §§18.8.1–18.8.2 Example 18.10
cards.title: Worked example: overlapping orders and sodium doublet resolution
cards.body: For 15,000 lines/inch, 2nd-order red (\(\lambda = 7\times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}, \theta_{2r} \approx 55.9^\circ\)) bends further than 3rd-order violet (\(\lambda = 4\times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}, \theta_{3v} \approx 45.2^\circ\)), so orders 2 and 3 overlap. Resolving sodium \(D_1, D_2\) (\(\Delta\lambda = 6\text{ \AA}\)) in 1st order requires \(N \ge 1000\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In an \(N\)-slit pattern, how many secondary minima lie between two adjacent principal maxima?
cards.why: Minima occur at \(N\gamma = p\pi\) for \(p = 1, 2, \dots, N - 1\), giving \(N - 1\) secondary minima between adjacent principal maxima (§18.7.1).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: How does a grating's angular dispersion \(\Delta\theta / \Delta\lambda\) depend on grating element \(d\)?
cards.why: From \(\Delta\theta / \Delta\lambda = m / (d\cos\theta)\), a smaller grating element \(d\) produces a larger angular dispersion (Eq. 18.65).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A grating with \(N = 1500\) illuminated lines is used in order \(m = 2\). Find resolving power \(R\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Rowland's grating has \(d = 1.759\times 10^{-4}\text{ cm}\). For \(\lambda = 6\times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}\), find the highest visible order \(m\).
cards.why: Since \(\sin\theta \le 1\), \(m \le d/\lambda = 1.759\times 10^{-4} / (6\times 10^{-5}) = 2.93\), so the maximum integer order is \(2\) (§18.8).

sections.title: Fresnel Diffraction, Zone Plate & Straight Edge

cards.title: Slicing a wavefront into concentric rings that alternate in sign
cards.meaning: Fresnel sliced a plane wavefront into bullseye rings whose distances to screen point P grow by λ/2 from one ring to the next, so adjacent rings arrive out of step by π.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><ellipse cx="68" cy="90" rx="26" ry="64" class="s ok"/><ellipse cx="68" cy="90" rx="20" ry="49" class="lk"/><ellipse cx="68" cy="90" rx="13" ry="32" class="ik"/><line x1="68" y1="90" x2="222" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="68" y1="41" x2="222" y2="90" class="ik"/><line x1="68" y1="26" x2="222" y2="90" class="lk"/><circle cx="68" cy="90" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="222" cy="90" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="54" y="94" class="t">O</text><text x="68" y="18" text-anchor="middle" class="t">W (r_n ≈ √(nλd))</text><text x="145" y="106" text-anchor="middle" class="t">d</text><text x="154" y="48" text-anchor="middle" class="t">d + nλ/2</text><text x="232" y="94" class="t">P</text><text x="148" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">u(P) = u₁ - u₂ + u₃ - u₄ + … ≈ u₁/2</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the concentric Fresnel zones on wavefront WW': each outer circle is λ/2 farther from P than the previous circle.
cards.example: Every zone has the same area πλd, but amplitudes slowly decrease (u₁ > u₂ > u₃ > …) because outer zones tilt at a larger obliquity angle χ.
cards.bridge: By Schuster's pairing method, the alternating series u₁ - u₂ + u₃ - u₄ + … for the whole unobstructed wavefront sums to u₁ / 2.

cards.label: 01 · §20.2 Definition
cards.title: What are Fresnel half-period zones?
cards.body: Fresnel half-period zones are annular rings on a plane wavefront bounded by circles at distances d + nλ/2 from P. Each zone has radius r_n ≈ √(nλd), equal area πλd, and is π out of phase with its neighbours.
cards.tex: r_n \approx \sqrt{n\lambda d}, \quad A_n \approx \pi\lambda d, \quad u(P) = u_1 - u_2 + u_3 - u_4 + \dots \approx \frac{u_1}{2}

cards.label: 02 · §20.2 Derivation
cards.title: Radius, equal area, and Schuster sum of Fresnel half-period zones
cards.legend: Plane wavefront at distance \(PO = d \gg \lambda\), \(n\)-th circle radius \(r_n\), zone area \(A_n\), and zone amplitudes \(u_1 > u_2 > u_3 > \dots\) (Eqs. 20.1–20.12, Fig. 20.2).

phases.name: Zone radius
phases.why: use right triangle POQ_n with d ≫ λ to find r_n ≈ √(nλd)

phases.name: Zone area
phases.why: subtract πr_{n-1}² from πr_n² to show all zones have area πλd

phases.name: Alternating sum
phases.why: sum consecutive zone amplitudes with alternating signs

phases.name: Schuster sum
phases.why: pair half-amplitudes to show the whole wavefront gives u₁/2

steps.note: In right triangle \(POQ_n\), the outer radius \(r_n\) of the \(n\)-th zone satisfies Pythagoras' theorem (Fig. 20.2).
Expand \((d + n\lambda/2)^2\) and cancel \(d^2 - d^2\).

ask.q: For visible light where \(d \gg \lambda\), which term is negligible?
ask.why: Since \(d \gg \lambda\) and \(n\) is not very large, \(n\lambda/(4d) \ll 1\), so \(n^2\lambda^2/4\) is negligible.

move.label: Neglect n²λ²/4 for d ≫ λ and take the square root (Eq. 20.1)

steps.note: Thus the radii of Fresnel half-period zones are proportional to \(\sqrt{n}\) (Eq. 20.1).

ask.q: How is the area \(A_n\) of the \(n\)-th annular zone defined?
ask.why: The \(n\)-th zone is the ring between circles \(r_n\) and \(r_{n-1}\), so its area is \(\pi r_n^2 - \pi r_{n-1}^2\).

move.label: Write area A_n of the n-th annular ring (Eq. 20.2)

steps.note: The \(n\)-th half-period zone is the annular region between the \(n\)-th and \((n-1)\)-th circles.
Substitute \(r_n^2 = n\lambda d\) and \(r_{n-1}^2 = (n-1)\lambda d\); every zone has the same area \(\pi\lambda d\) (Eq. 20.2).

ask.q: Why do consecutive zones contribute with alternating signs in \(u(P)\)?
options: Light travels backward from even zones
ask.why: Corresponding points \(Q_n\) and \(Q_{n-1}\) satisfy \(Q_n P - Q_{n-1} P = \lambda/2\), which is a phase difference of \(\pi\).

move.label: Sum zone amplitudes with alternating signs at P (Eq. 20.3)

steps.note: Due to increased obliquity \(\chi\), amplitudes decrease slowly: \(u_1 > u_2 > u_3 > \dots\) (Eqs. 20.3–20.5).

move.label: Group terms by Schuster's method (Eq. 20.6)

steps.note: Rewrite Eq. (20.3) by splitting odd terms into halves and bracketing around each even term (Eq. 20.6).

ask.q: Since \(u_n \approx \frac{1}{2}(u_{n-1} + u_{n+1})\) and \(u_m \to 0\), what is \(u(P)\)?
ask.why: The bracketed terms cancel and \(u_m \to 0\) for the full wavefront, leaving \(u(P) \approx u_1 / 2\) (Eq. 20.12).

steps.note: The resultant amplitude of the entire unobstructed wavefront is half the amplitude of the first zone alone (Eq. 20.12).

cards.title: A circular hole can make the center dark, and a solid coin makes it bright!
cards.meaning: Opening just 1 Fresnel zone gives amplitude u₁ = 2(u₁/2) and intensity 4I₀; opening 2 zones gives u₁ - u₂ ≈ 0 (dark); and blocking the first p zones with a solid disc always leaves u_{p+1}/2 (a bright Poisson spot!).
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="18" y1="90" x2="224" y2="90" class="gk"/><ellipse cx="74" cy="90" rx="16" ry="42" class="s ok"/><line x1="214" y1="22" x2="214" y2="158" class="ik"/><line x1="20" y1="58" x2="66" y2="58" class="lk"/><line x1="20" y1="122" x2="66" y2="122" class="lk"/><line x1="74" y1="48" x2="214" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="74" y1="132" x2="214" y2="90" class="lk"/><circle cx="214" cy="90" r="4.5" class="f"/><text x="74" y="152" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Opaque disc (blocks p zones)</text><text x="164" y="42" text-anchor="middle" class="t">u(P) = u_{p+1} - u_{p+2} + …</text><text x="164" y="60" text-anchor="middle" class="t">≈ u_{p+1} / 2</text><text x="224" y="94" class="t">P (Bright!)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the opaque disc blocking the first p zones: waves from the (p + 1)-th zone around the rim meet in phase at axial point P.
cards.example: In 1818 Poisson predicted this bright spot to disprove Fresnel's wave theory, but Arago immediately saw the spot at the shadow center!
cards.bridge: For a circular hole of radius a, axial maxima occur when a² = (2n + 1)λd (odd zones) and minima when a² = 2nλd (even zones).

cards.label: 03 · §§20.2.1–20.2.2 Definition
cards.title: What is the Poisson spot and circular-aperture axial diffraction?
cards.body: A circular hole of radius a gives axial maxima for odd numbers of zones (1st zone alone gives u₁ and intensity 4I₀) and minima for even numbers of zones. An opaque disc blocking p zones always leaves u_{p+1}/2, forming a bright Poisson spot.

cards.title: Blackening every second zone to build a flat diffraction lens
cards.meaning: A zone plate blocks all the even-numbered zones (-u₂, -u₄, …) so all the odd-numbered zones (+u₁ + u₃ + u₅ + …) arrive in step and create a brilliant focus!
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="66" cy="90" r="52" class="s ok"/><circle cx="66" cy="90" r="45" class="lk"/><circle cx="66" cy="90" r="37" class="s ok"/><circle cx="66" cy="90" r="26" class="lk"/><line x1="132" y1="90" x2="244" y2="90" class="gk"/><line x1="132" y1="38" x2="132" y2="142" class="ik"/><line x1="132" y1="46" x2="232" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="132" y1="134" x2="232" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="132" y1="46" x2="166" y2="90" class="ik"/><line x1="132" y1="134" x2="166" y2="90" class="ik"/><circle cx="232" cy="90" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="166" cy="90" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="182" cy="90" r="3" class="f"/><text x="66" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">r_n = √n K</text><text x="166" y="108" text-anchor="middle" class="t">P₃ (f/3)</text><text x="184" y="76" text-anchor="middle" class="t">P₂ (dark)</text><text x="226" y="108" text-anchor="middle" class="t">P₁ (f = K²/λ)</text><text x="190" y="32" text-anchor="middle" class="t">u(P₁) = u₁ + u₃ + u₅ + …</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the zone plate (left) and its axis (right): odd zones add to an intense primary focus at P₁ (f = K²/λ) and weaker odd foci at f/3, f/5, …
cards.example: At P₃ = K²/(3λ), each ring holds 3 half-period zones, so (u₁ - u₂ + u₃) + (u₇ - u₈ + u₉) + … gives a weaker secondary focus.
cards.bridge: For a point source S at distance a and image P at distance b, requiring the first zone edge L to add path λ/2 gives the lens-like formula 1/a + 1/b = 1/f.

cards.label: 04 · §20.3 Definition
cards.title: What is a Fresnel zone plate?
cards.body: A zone plate consists of concentric circles of radii r_n = √n K with alternate annular zones blackened. For an incident plane wave, it forms an intense primary focus at f = K²/λ and weaker foci at K²/(3λ), K²/(5λ), …

cards.label: 05 · §20.3 Derivation
cards.title: Zone-plate imaging formula 1/a + 1/b = 1/f
cards.legend: Point source \(S\) at distance \(a\) on the axis, zone plate of first-circle radius \(r_1\) at point \(L\), and bright image \(P\) at distance \(b\) (Eqs. 20.18–20.20).

phases.name: Half-wave path
phases.why: require path difference SL + LP - SP = λ/2 at the rim L of the first circle

phases.name: Pythagoras
phases.why: express SL and LP using right triangles with height r₁

phases.name: Binomial
phases.why: expand the square roots for r₁ ≪ a, b and cancel a + b

phases.name: Lens-like law
phases.why: divide by r₁² / 2 and define focal length f = r₁² / λ

steps.note: For the first circle (radius \(r_1\)) to enclose the first half-period zone, point \(L\) must add path \(\lambda/2\) (Eq. 20.18).
Substitute the hypotenuse lengths \(SL\) and \(LP\) and axial distance \(SP = a + b\).

ask.q: In the paraxial limit \(r_1 \ll a\), what approximates \(\sqrt{a^2 + r_1^2}\)?
ask.why: Factoring out \(a\) and using \((1 + x)^{1/2} \approx 1 + x/2\) gives \(a[1 + r_1^2/(2a^2)] = a + r_1^2/(2a)\).

steps.note: Apply the binomial approximation \((1 + x)^{1/2} \approx 1 + x/2\) to both square roots.
Cancel \(a + b - (a + b)\) and factor out \(r_1^2 / 2\) (Eq. 20.19).

ask.q: Which move isolates \(1/a + 1/b\) on the left-hand side?
ask.why: Dividing both sides by \(r_1^2 / 2\) cancels the prefactor and leaves \(\lambda / r_1^2\) on the right.

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(r_1^2 / 2\).

ask.q: Comparing \(1/a + 1/b = \lambda/r_1^2\) with \(1/a + 1/b = 1/f\), what is \(f\)?
ask.why: Matching \(1/f = \lambda / r_1^2\) defines the primary focal length \(f = r_1^2 / \lambda\) (Eq. 20.20).

steps.note: Thus a zone plate acts like a converging lens of primary focal length \(f = r_1^2 / \lambda\) (Eq. 20.20).

ask.q: Because \(f = r_1^2 / \lambda\) depends strongly on \(\lambda\), what aberration does a zone plate show?
ask.why: Since \(f\) is inversely proportional to wavelength \(\lambda\), different colors focus at very different distances (§20.3).

cards.label: 06 · §20.3 Examples 20.1–20.2
cards.title: Worked example: circular aperture extrema and zone-plate foci
cards.tex: OP_{\max} = \frac{(0.05)^2}{5\times 10^{-5}} = 50\text{ cm}, \quad OP_{\min} = \frac{(0.05)^2}{2\times 5\times 10^{-5}} = 25\text{ cm}; \quad f_1 = \frac{r_1^2}{\lambda} = \frac{0.01}{5\times 10^{-5}} = 200\text{ cm}
cards.body: For a circular hole of radius \(a = 0.5\text{ mm}\) and \(\lambda = 5\times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}\), the brightest axial point (1 zone) is at \(50\text{ cm}\) and the darkest point (2 zones) is at \(25\text{ cm}\). A zone plate with \(r_n = 0.1\sqrt{n}\text{ cm}\) has foci at \(200, 200/3, 200/5\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: If a circular aperture exposes only the first Fresnel zone, what is the intensity at \(P\)?
cards.why: The first zone gives amplitude \(u_1 = 2(u_1/2) = 2u_{\text{unobstructed}}\), so the intensity is \(2^2 I_0 = 4I_0\) (§20.2.1).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What happens at axial point \(P\) when a circular aperture contains the first two half-period zones?
cards.why: The first two zones are \(\pi\) out of phase and have nearly equal amplitudes, so \(u_1 - u_2 \approx 0\) (§20.2.1).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: The bright spot always formed on the axis behind an opaque circular disc is the ______ spot.
cards.why: If a disc blocks the first \(p\) zones, the remaining zones sum to \(u_{p+1}/2\), forming the bright Poisson spot (§20.2.2).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A zone plate has \(r_1 = 1\text{ mm}\) and \(\lambda = 500\text{ nm}\). Find its primary focal length \(f\) in m.
cards.why: \(f = \frac{r_1^2}{\lambda} = \frac{(10^{-3}\text{ m})^2}{5\times 10^{-7}\text{ m}} = 2\text{ m}\) (Example 20.2).

cards.title: Winding secondary wavelets into a double spiral (Cornu's spiral)
cards.meaning: As we move away from the pole of a wavefront, the extra path grows as u², making the phase turn faster and faster so the phasor chain curls into two tight eyes at C(1/2, 1/2) and C'(-1/2, -1/2).
cards.picture: Look at Cornu's spiral: the chord PC from point P(v₀) on the curve to the upper eye C(1/2, 1/2) gives the diffracted wave amplitude.
cards.example: For the whole unobstructed wavefront (from C' at -∞ to C at +∞), the chord C'C has components (1, 1) and length √2.
cards.bridge: The coordinates of any point τ on Cornu's spiral are the Fresnel integrals C(τ) = ∫₀^τ cos(πu²/2) du and S(τ) = ∫₀^τ sin(πu²/2) du.

cards.label: 01 · §20.6 Definition
cards.title: What are the Fresnel integrals and Cornu's spiral?
cards.body: Fresnel integrals C(τ) = ∫₀^τ cos(πu²/2)du and S(τ) = ∫₀^τ sin(πu²/2)du are odd functions with C(0)=S(0)=0 and C(∞)=S(∞)=1/2. Their parametric plot is Cornu's spiral, whose chord length gives wave amplitude.
cards.tex: C(\tau) = \int_0^\tau\cos\left(\frac{\pi u^2}{2}\right)du, \quad S(\tau) = \int_0^\tau\sin\left(\frac{\pi u^2}{2}\right)du, \quad C(\infty) = S(\infty) = \frac{1}{2}

cards.title: Why light leaks into the shadow and ripples outside a sharp edge
cards.meaning: At the exact shadow boundary (y = 0), a straight edge blocks the lower half of the wavefront, leaving half the amplitude (u₀/2) and one-fourth the intensity (I₀/4)!
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="64" y="96" width="12" height="68" class="s ok"/><line x1="64" y1="96" x2="214" y2="96" class="gk"/><line x1="214" y1="16" x2="214" y2="164" class="ik"/><line x1="20" y1="48" x2="64" y2="48" class="lk"/><line x1="20" y1="82" x2="64" y2="82" class="lk"/><line x1="20" y1="126" x2="60" y2="126" class="lk"/><line x1="70" y1="42" x2="214" y2="56" class="lk"/><circle cx="70" cy="42" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="214" cy="56" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="214" cy="96" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="214" cy="132" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="70" y="28" text-anchor="middle" class="t">M(ξ, η)</text><text x="142" y="40" text-anchor="middle" class="t">r</text><text x="142" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">d</text><text x="224" y="60" class="t">P(0, y) [Lit]</text><text x="224" y="100" class="t">O (I = I₀/4)</text><text x="224" y="136" class="t">Q [Shadow]</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the straight edge blocking η < 0: at O (y = 0) intensity is I₀/4, below O it fades to zero, and above O it forms bright and dark fringes.
cards.example: As we move into the illuminated region (y > 0, v₀ < 0), the chord PC on Cornu's spiral stretches to 1.66 at v₀ ≈ -1.22, giving first peak I ≈ 1.37 I₀.
cards.bridge: Integrating over the open upper half-plane (ξ from -∞ to +∞, η from 0 to +∞) gives I(P) = ½ I₀{[½ - C(v₀)]² + [½ - S(v₀)]²}.

cards.label: 02 · §20.6 Definition
cards.title: What is the straight-edge Fresnel diffraction pattern?
cards.body: For a plane wave incident on a straight edge at distance d from the screen, intensity is I₀/4 on the shadow edge (y = 0), decays monotonically to 0 in the shadow (y < 0), and oscillates (peaking at 1.37 I₀) for y > 0.

cards.label: 03 · §20.6 Derivation
cards.title: Straight-edge Fresnel diffraction field and intensity
cards.legend: Aperture point \(M(\xi, \eta)\) with \(\eta \ge 0\), screen point \(P(0, y)\) at distance \(d\), and lower Fresnel limit \(v_0 = -\sqrt{\frac{2}{\lambda d}}\,y\) (Eqs. 20.49–20.59, Fig. 20.12).

phases.name: Paraxial distance
phases.why: expand r = MP for d ≫ ξ, η - y

phases.name: Fresnel variables
phases.why: define dimensionless variables u, v and lower limit v₀ at η = 0

phases.name: Evaluate integrals
phases.why: express the u and v integrals using C(∞)=S(∞)=1/2 and C(v₀), S(v₀)

phases.name: Intensity & shadow edge
phases.why: take the squared modulus for I(P) and evaluate at y = 0

steps.note: Expand \(r = MP = [\xi^2 + (\eta - y)^2 + d^2]^{1/2}\) for \(d \gg \xi, \eta - y\) (Eq. 20.49).
At the straight edge \(\eta = 0\), the lower limit of \(v\) is \(v_0 = -\sqrt{2/(\lambda d)}\,y\) (Eqs. 20.51, 20.53).

ask.q: When observation point \(P\) lies on the shadow edge \(y = 0\), what is \(v_0\)?
ask.why: Substituting \(y = 0\) into \(v_0 = -\sqrt{2/(\lambda d)}\,y\) gives \(v_0 = 0\) (Eq. 20.53).

move.label: Write the Fresnel diffraction integral over u and v (Eq. 20.52)

steps.note: Here \(u_0 = Ae^{ikd}\) is the unobstructed field at \(P\) (Eq. 20.52).
Since \(2[C(\infty) + iS(\infty)] = 2(1/2 + i/2) = 1 + i\), the \(u\)-integral equals \(1 + i\) (Eq. 20.54).

ask.q: Splitting \(\int_{v_0}^{\infty}\) as \(\int_0^{\infty} - \int_0^{v_0}\), what is its real part?

steps.note: Substitute both integrals and use \(-\frac{i}{2}(1 + i) = \frac{1 - i}{2}\) (Eq. 20.56).

ask.q: What is the squared modulus \(|(1 - i)/2|^2\) of the prefactor in \(u(P)\)?

move.label: Take the squared modulus |u(P)|² to obtain intensity I(P) (Eq. 20.58)

steps.note: This gives the intensity at any point \(P\) in terms of the chord length \(PC\) on Cornu's spiral (Eq. 20.58).

ask.q: At the shadow boundary \(y = 0\) (\(v_0 = 0, C(0) = S(0) = 0\)), what is \(I(P)\)?

steps.note: Right on the edge of the geometrical shadow, the intensity is one-fourth of the unobstructed intensity \(I_0\) (Eq. 20.59).

cards.label: 04 · §20.6 Intensity graph
cards.title: Universal straight-edge intensity curve I/I₀ (Fig. 20.13)
cards.body: Plotted against √(2/λd) y = -v₀, intensity is 0.25 I₀ at y = 0, drops smoothly to 0 in the shadow (y < 0), and oscillates in the lit region with maxima 1.37 I₀ (-v₀ ≈ 1.22), 1.20 I₀ (2.34), and first minimum 0.778 I₀ (1.87).

cards.label: 05 · §20.6 Numerical example
cards.title: Worked example: positions of straight-edge maxima and minima
cards.body: For \(\lambda = 6\times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}\) and \(d = 120\text{ cm}\), \(\sqrt{\lambda d / 2} = 0.06\text{ cm} = 0.6\text{ mm}\). The first three maxima (\(v_0 = -1.22, -2.34, -3.08\)) occur at \(y \approx 0.732, 1.404, 1.848\text{ mm}\), and the first three minima (\(v_0 = -1.87, -2.74, -3.39\)) at \(1.122, 1.644, 2.034\text{ mm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the intensity right on the edge of the geometrical shadow (\(y = 0\)) of a straight edge?

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: How does the intensity vary as we move deeper into the geometrical shadow of a straight edge?
cards.why: As \(v_0 > 0\) increases into the shadow, point \(Q\) spirals smoothly toward \(C(1/2, 1/2)\) and chord \(QC\) decreases monotonically to zero (§20.6).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: What is the limiting value of the Fresnel integral \(C(\infty)\) (or \(S(\infty)\)) as a decimal?
cards.why: Both Fresnel integrals converge to \(C(\infty) = S(\infty) = 1/2 = 0.5\) (Eq. 20.47).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: In straight-edge diffraction with \(\sqrt{\lambda d / 2} = 1\text{ mm}\), find the first maximum position \(y_1\) (\(v_0 = -1.22\)) in mm.

sheets.title: Polarisation: introduction
sheets.source: Unit 17 · Ghatak ch. 22 §22.1 (PDF pp. 355–357; Book 2 not available); syllabus item 17

cards.title: Shaking a string in one flat plane or in a circle
cards.meaning: A linearly polarised wave vibrates back and forth along one fixed straight line at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="14" width="112" height="152" rx="12" class="s ok"/><rect x="136" y="14" width="112" height="152" rx="12" class="s ok"/><line x1="22" y1="96" x2="116" y2="96" class="gk"/><line x1="30" y1="140" x2="30" y2="44" class="gk"/><path d="M 30 96 Q 48 44 66 96 T 102 96" class="lk"/><circle cx="48" cy="70" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="68" y="32" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Linear (x-z plane)</text><text x="68" y="156" text-anchor="middle" class="t">y(z, t) = 0</text><circle cx="192" cy="92" r="34" class="lk"/><line x1="148" y1="92" x2="236" y2="92" class="gk"/><line x1="192" y1="48" x2="192" y2="136" class="gk"/><line x1="192" y1="92" x2="216" y2="68" class="ik"/><circle cx="216" cy="68" r="4" class="f"/><text x="192" y="32" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Circular (radius a)</text><text x="192" y="156" text-anchor="middle" class="t">x² + y² = a²</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare the left box (string vibrating straight up and down along x) with the right box (string end rotating on a circle of radius a).
cards.example: When you shake a rope purely up and down, y = 0 everywhere; when you swing the end in a circle, every point traces a circle of radius a.
cards.bridge: Combining x = a cos(kz - ωt + φ) and y = -a sin(kz - ωt + φ) with a 90° phase shift gives x² + y² = a², a right-circularly polarised wave.

cards.label: 01 · §22.1 Definition
cards.title: What are linearly and circularly polarised waves?
cards.body: In a linearly (plane) polarised wave, vibrations stay on one line in the x-z or y-z plane. In a circularly polarised wave, each point moves on a circle of radius a.

cards.label: 02 · §22.1 Derivation
cards.title: Circularly polarised wave path from orthogonal components
cards.legend: Transverse displacements \(x(z,t)\) and \(y(z,t)\) with equal amplitude \(a\) and a \(90^\circ\) phase difference (Eq. 22.3, Fig. 22.2).

phases.name: Components
phases.why: write the x and y displacements with a 90° phase difference

phases.name: Square components
phases.why: square x and y so sin and cos become squared

phases.name: Combine
phases.why: add x² and y² and factor out a²

phases.name: Circle law
phases.why: use cos² + sin² = 1 to get a circle of radius a

steps.note: Start with the \(x\)-component of displacement (Eq. 22.3).

move.label: Write y-component shifted in phase by 90° (Eq. 22.3)

steps.note: The \(y\)-component has the same amplitude \(a\) and a \(90^\circ\) phase shift (Eq. 22.3).

ask.q: How do we eliminate the time-dependent angle \((kz - \omega t + \phi)\)?
ask.why: Squaring \(x\) and \(y\) and adding uses \(\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1\) to remove the phase angle.

move.label: Square the x-component equation

steps.note: Square both sides of the \(x\)-displacement equation.

move.label: Square the y-component equation

steps.note: Squaring \(-a\sin(kz - \omega t + \phi)\) makes the minus sign positive.

ask.q: When \(y = -a\sin(kz - \omega t + \phi)\) is squared, what is \(y^2\)?
ask.why: Since \((-a)^2 = +a^2\), squaring \(y\) gives \(a^2\sin^2(kz - \omega t + \phi)\).

steps.tex: x^2 + y^2 = a^2\cos^2(kz - \omega t + \phi) + a^2\sin^2(kz - \omega t + \phi)
steps.note: Add the \(x^2\) and \(y^2\) equations together.
Factor out the common squared amplitude \(a^2\).

ask.q: What does \(\cos^2(kz - \omega t + \phi) + \sin^2(kz - \omega t + \phi)\) equal?
ask.why: By the Pythagorean trigonometric identity, \(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\) at every instant.

steps.note: Each point on the string moves on a circle of constant radius \(a\) (Eq. 22.3).

ask.q: What path does \(x^2 + y^2 = a^2\) describe in the \(x\text{-}y\) plane?
ask.why: Constant \(x^2 + y^2 = a^2\) is the equation of a circle of radius \(a\) centered on the \(z\)-axis.

cards.title: How two narrow slits or Polaroids prove light is transverse
cards.meaning: Unpolarised light has an electric field that jumps randomly to new transverse directions every tiny fraction of a second.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="18" y1="90" x2="242" y2="90" class="gk"/><line x1="38" y1="62" x2="38" y2="118" class="lk"/><line x1="14" y1="90" x2="62" y2="90" class="lk"/><line x1="20" y1="72" x2="56" y2="108" class="ik"/><line x1="20" y1="108" x2="56" y2="72" class="ik"/><rect x="92" y="36" width="18" height="108" rx="4" class="s ok"/><line x1="101" y1="46" x2="101" y2="134" class="lk"/><line x1="144" y1="56" x2="144" y2="124" class="lk"/><rect x="184" y="58" width="42" height="64" rx="4" class="s ok"/><line x1="192" y1="90" x2="218" y2="90" class="ik"/><text x="38" y="142" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Unpolarised</text><text x="101" y="28" text-anchor="middle" class="t">P₁ (Polariser)</text><text x="144" y="46" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Linear E</text><text x="205" y="48" text-anchor="middle" class="t">P₂ (Analyser)</text><text x="205" y="142" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Crossed → 0</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at unpolarised light (left star) passing P₁ to become vertically polarised, then blocked when analyser P₂ is turned horizontal.
cards.example: If light were a longitudinal wave (vibrating along z), rotating the second Polaroid P₂ would never change the transmitted brightness.
cards.bridge: In Maxwell's electromagnetic wave along z, E (along x) and H (along y) are both perpendicular to z, with E_z = H_z = 0.

cards.label: 03 · §22.1 Definition
cards.title: What is unpolarised light and a Polaroid pass axis?
cards.body: In unpolarised light, the transverse electric vector E changes direction randomly. A Polaroid absorbs E along one axis and transmits E along its perpendicular pass axis.
cards.tex: E_x = E_0\cos(kz - \omega t), \quad H_y = H_0\cos(kz - \omega t), \quad E_z = H_z = 0

cards.label: 04 · §22.1 Electromagnetic wave
cards.title: Transverse electric and magnetic fields in a dielectric (Eqs. 22.4–22.8)
cards.body: For an \(x\)-polarised plane wave propagating along \(+z\) (along \(\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H}\)), \(\mathbf{E}\) lies along \(x\), \(\mathbf{H}\) lies along \(y\), and the intrinsic impedance of free space is \(\eta_0 \approx 120\pi\,\Omega\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Which property of light is proved when rotating a second Polaroid causes darkness?
cards.why: Only a transverse wave changes its transmitted amplitude when the orientation of a slit or Polaroid is rotated (§22.1).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In an electromagnetic wave with \(\mathbf{E}\) along \(x\) and \(\mathbf{H}\) along \(y\), light travels along:
cards.why: Vectors \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{H}\) are perpendicular to each other and the wave propagates along \(\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H}\) (§22.1).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: The direction of the electric vector transmitted by a Polaroid is called its ______ axis.
cards.why: A Polaroid absorbs the component of \(\mathbf{E}\) along one direction and transmits the perpendicular component along its pass axis (§22.1).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A circularly polarised wave on a string has amplitude \(a = 3\text{ cm}\). Find \(x^2 + y^2\) in \(\text{cm}^2\).
