sheets.source: Unit 18 · Ghatak ch. 22 §22.3 (PDF pp. 358–360; Book 2 not available); syllabus item 18

cards.title: Why parallel wires block the electric component parallel to them
cards.meaning: A wire-grid polariser or Polaroid sheet uses parallel conducting lines that let electrons slide along them, absorbing the parallel electric field as heat.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="18" y1="90" x2="242" y2="90" class="gk"/><line x1="42" y1="56" x2="42" y2="124" class="lk"/><line x1="16" y1="90" x2="68" y2="90" class="ik"/><rect x="102" y="28" width="48" height="124" rx="4" class="s ok"/><line x1="112" y1="28" x2="112" y2="152" class="ik"/><line x1="122" y1="28" x2="122" y2="152" class="ik"/><line x1="132" y1="28" x2="132" y2="152" class="ik"/><line x1="142" y1="28" x2="142" y2="152" class="ik"/><line x1="182" y1="90" x2="234" y2="90" class="lk"/><circle cx="182" cy="90" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="234" cy="90" r="3" class="f"/><text x="42" y="46" text-anchor="middle" class="t">E_x and E_y</text><text x="126" y="20" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Wires along y (E_y absorbed)</text><text x="208" y="72" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Emergent E_x</text><text x="208" y="114" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(Pass axis ⊥ wires)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the vertical wires along y: the vertical E_y drives currents in the wires and is absorbed, while horizontal E_x passes through.
cards.example: A 3 cm microwave wire grid is easy to build because wire spacing only needs to be less than 3 cm; for visible light, a Polaroid uses aligned iodine polymer chains.
cards.bridge: Therefore the pass axis of a wire-grid polariser or Polaroid is always perpendicular to the aligned conducting wires or polymer molecules.

cards.label: 01 · §22.3.1 Definition
cards.title: What are a wire-grid polariser and a Polaroid?
cards.body: A wire-grid polariser has parallel wires spaced less than λ that absorb E parallel to the wires by Joule heating and transmit E perpendicular. A Polaroid uses aligned iodine polymer chains.

cards.title: Reflecting light at Brewster's angle so only one polarisation bounces
cards.meaning: Brewster's law gives the special incidence angle θ_p where the electric field vibrating in the plane of incidence has zero reflection.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="20" y="96" width="220" height="64" class="s ok"/><line x1="130" y1="18" x2="130" y2="164" class="gk"/><line x1="46" y1="32" x2="130" y2="96" class="lk"/><line x1="130" y1="96" x2="214" y2="32" class="lk"/><line x1="130" y1="96" x2="178" y2="158" class="ik"/><circle cx="158" cy="75" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="182" cy="56" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="202" cy="41" r="3" class="f"/><text x="34" y="84" class="t">n₁</text><text x="34" y="118" class="t">n₂</text><text x="114" y="56" class="t">θ_p</text><text x="144" y="56" class="t">θ_p</text><text x="142" y="138" class="t">θ_r</text><text x="206" y="76" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Reflected (s-polarised)</text><text x="190" y="114" class="t">90°</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the interface at Brewster's angle θ_p: the reflected ray (dots, perpendicular to the page) and refracted ray are 90° apart.
cards.example: Sunlight reflecting off water (n₂ = 1.33) near θ_p ≈ 53° is horizontally polarised glare, which vertically polarised sunglasses block.
cards.bridge: Combining Brewster's law tan θ_p = n₂/n₁ with Snell's law n₁ sin θ_p = n₂ sin θ_r proves that cos θ_p = sin θ_r, so θ_p + θ_r = 90°.

cards.label: 02 · §22.3.2 Definition
cards.title: What is Brewster's law?
cards.body: Brewster's law states that when unpolarised light hits an interface at θ_p = tan⁻¹(n₂/n₁), the reflected ray is linearly polarised perpendicular to the plane of incidence and is 90° to the refracted ray.

cards.label: 03 · §22.3.2 Derivation
cards.title: Brewster's law and right angle between reflected and refracted rays
cards.legend: Dielectric interface between \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) with polarising angle \(\theta_p\) and refraction angle \(\theta_r\) (Eq. 22.10, Fig. 22.9).

phases.name: Brewster's law
phases.why: write tan θ_p = n₂ / n₁ as sin θ_p / cos θ_p

phases.name: Snell's law
phases.why: equate the Brewster ratio to Snell's law sin θ_p / sin θ_r

phases.name: Equate cosines
phases.why: cancel sin θ_p and take reciprocals to get sin θ_r = cos θ_p

phases.name: Right angle
phases.why: replace cos θ_p by sin(90° - θ_p) to show θ_p + θ_r = 90°

steps.note: Start from Brewster's law at the polarising angle \(\theta_p\) (Eq. 22.10).
Rewrite \(\tan\theta_p\) as \(\sin\theta_p / \cos\theta_p\).

ask.q: By Snell's law at angle \(\theta_p\), what else equals \(n_2 / n_1\)?
ask.why: Snell's law \(n_1\sin\theta_p = n_2\sin\theta_r\) gives \(n_2/n_1 = \sin\theta_p/\sin\theta_r\).

move.label: Write Snell's law at incidence angle θ_p

steps.note: Write Snell's law of refraction for the transmitted ray at angle \(\theta_r\).
Equate the two expressions for \(n_2 / n_1\).

ask.q: Which move cancels \(\sin\theta_p\) from the numerators?
ask.why: Since \(\sin\theta_p \neq 0\), dividing both sides by \(\sin\theta_p\) leaves \(1/\sin\theta_r = 1/\cos\theta_p\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(\sin\theta_p\).
Take the reciprocal of both sides.

ask.q: Which cofunction identity rewrites \(\cos\theta_p\) as a sine?
ask.why: For complementary angles, \(\cos\theta_p = \sin(90^\circ - \theta_p)\).

steps.note: Replace \(\cos\theta_p\) with \(\sin(90^\circ - \theta_p)\).

ask.q: Since \(\theta_r = 90^\circ - \theta_p\), what is the angle between the reflected and refracted rays?
ask.why: Along the normal, \(180^\circ - (\theta_p + \theta_r) = 180^\circ - 90^\circ = 90^\circ\) (§22.3.2).

move.label: Equate acute angles and add θ_p to both sides

steps.note: At Brewster's angle, the reflected and transmitted rays are at right angles (§22.3.2).

cards.title: Eliminating one of the two crystal beams by absorption or reflection
cards.meaning: When a crystal splits light into two polarised beams, we obtain one clean polarised beam either by absorbing one beam (dichroism) or reflecting it aside (Nicol prism).
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="24" width="96" height="132" rx="10" class="s ok"/><polygon points="140,136 160,44 238,44 218,136" class="s ok"/><line x1="140" y1="136" x2="238" y2="44" class="gk"/><line x1="18" y1="90" x2="102" y2="72" class="lk"/><line x1="18" y1="90" x2="64" y2="114" class="ik"/><line x1="124" y1="96" x2="188" y2="80" class="lk"/><line x1="188" y1="80" x2="248" y2="80" class="lk"/><line x1="124" y1="96" x2="180" y2="98" class="ik"/><line x1="180" y1="98" x2="196" y2="144" class="ik"/><text x="62" y="42" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Tourmaline</text><text x="62" y="146" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Dichroism</text><text x="190" y="32" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Nicol prism (Canada balsam)</text><text x="232" y="70" text-anchor="middle" class="t">e-ray</text><text x="204" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">o-ray (TIR)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare tourmaline on the left (absorbs one beam by dichroism) with the Nicol prism on the right (Canada balsam layer reflects the o-ray by total internal reflection).
cards.example: In a Nicol prism, Canada balsam has a refractive index between n_o and n_e, so it acts as a rarer medium for the o-ray and reflects it away.
cards.bridge: A fourth method is scattering (§22.3.4): unpolarised light scattered at 90° by gas molecules is linearly polarised because light waves are transverse.

cards.label: 04 · §§22.3.3–22.3.4 Definition
cards.title: What are dichroism, a Nicol prism, and scattering polarisation?
cards.body: Dichroism is selective absorption of one polarised beam (as in tourmaline). A Nicol prism uses Canada balsam to remove the ordinary ray by total internal reflection. Gas scattering at 90° is also linearly polarised.

cards.label: 05 · §22.3.2 Worked example
cards.title: Brewster angle for air-water interface and polarised sunglasses (§22.3.2)
cards.body: For sunlight hitting water (\(n_1 \approx 1, n_2 \approx 1.33\)) near \(\theta_p \approx 53^\circ\), the reflected glare is horizontally polarised (perpendicular to the vertical plane of incidence). Polarised sunglasses have a vertical pass axis to block this horizontal glare.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In a wire-grid polariser with wires along \(y\), which electric component passes through?
cards.why: Currents along the \(y\)-wires absorb \(E_y\) by Joule heating, while \(E_x\) perpendicular to the wires passes through (§22.3.1).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: At Brewster's angle \(\theta_p\), what is the angle between the reflected and transmitted rays?
cards.why: Since \(\tan\theta_p = n_2/n_1 = \sin\theta_p/\sin\theta_r\), \(\cos\theta_p = \sin\theta_r\), so the reflected and transmitted rays are at \(90^\circ\) (§22.3.2).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Selective absorption of one polarised beam in a crystal like tourmaline is called ______.
cards.why: The property of selectively absorbing one of the two doubly refracted polarised beams is called dichroism (§22.3.3).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Light in air (\(n_1 = 1\)) hits glass of index \(n_2 = \sqrt{3}\) at Brewster's angle. Find \(\theta_p\) in degrees.
cards.why: From \(\tan\theta_p = n_2/n_1 = \sqrt{3}\), \(\theta_p = \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3}) = 60^\circ\).

sheets.title: Polariser, analyser & Malus's law
sheets.source: Unit 19 · Ghatak ch. 22 §22.2 (PDF pp. 358–360; Book 2 not available); syllabus item 19

cards.title: Resolving the electric field along a tilted analyser
cards.meaning: When a linearly polarised wave of amplitude E₀ hits a second Polaroid tilted at angle θ, only the component E₀ cos θ parallel to the new pass axis gets through.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="130" cy="94" r="62" class="s ok"/><line x1="56" y1="94" x2="204" y2="94" class="gk"/><line x1="130" y1="24" x2="130" y2="164" class="lk"/><line x1="130" y1="94" x2="178" y2="46" class="ik"/><line x1="130" y1="36" x2="168" y2="56" class="gk"/><path d="M 130 62 A 32 32 0 0 1 152 71" class="lk"/><circle cx="130" cy="36" r="4" class="f"/><circle cx="168" cy="56" r="4" class="f"/><text x="116" y="38" text-anchor="end" class="t">E₀ (from P₁)</text><text x="142" y="56" class="t">θ</text><text x="184" y="52" class="t">P₂ pass axis</text><text x="184" y="72" class="t">E₀ cos θ</text><text x="130" y="174" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Intensity I ∝ (E₀ cos θ)² → I = I₀ cos²θ</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at vertical amplitude E₀ from P₁ projected onto the tilted pass axis of analyser P₂ to give transmitted amplitude E₀ cos θ.
cards.example: At θ = 60°, cos 60° = 1/2 so the electric field amplitude drops to E₀/2 and the intensity drops to (1/2)² I₀ = I₀/4.
cards.bridge: Because light intensity is proportional to the square of electric field amplitude, squaring E₀ cos θ gives Malus's law I = I₀ cos²θ.

cards.label: 01 · §22.2 Definition
cards.title: What is Malus's law?
cards.body: Malus's law states that when a linearly polarised beam of intensity I₀ falls on an analyser whose pass axis makes an angle θ with the incident electric vector, the emergent intensity is I = I₀ cos²θ.

cards.label: 02 · §22.2 Derivation
cards.title: Malus's law for intensity transmitted by an analyser
cards.legend: Incident linearly polarised wave of amplitude \(E_0\) along \(x\) (intensity \(I_0 = K E_0^2\)) incident on analyser \(P_2\) at angle \(\theta\) (Eq. 22.9, Fig. 22.6).

phases.name: Resolve field
phases.why: resolve incident amplitude E₀ along and perpendicular to P₂'s pass axis

phases.name: Square amplitude
phases.why: square the transmitted electric field component E_∥

phases.name: Intensity ratio
phases.why: multiply by proportionality constant K so I = K E_∥²

phases.name: Malus's law
phases.why: substitute I₀ = K E₀² to obtain I = I₀ cos²θ

steps.note: Resolve the incident electric field \(E_0\) along the pass axis of analyser \(P_2\) at angle \(\theta\).

move.label: Write perpendicular component absorbed by analyser P₂

steps.note: The perpendicular component \(E_0\sin\theta\) is absorbed by \(P_2\), so only \(E_\parallel\) emerges.

ask.q: Which component of \(E_0\) is transmitted by the analyser \(P_2\)?
ask.why: The analyser transmits only the component \(E_0\cos\theta\) parallel to its pass axis (§22.2).

move.label: Square both sides of E_∥ = E₀ cos θ

steps.note: Square the emergent amplitude \(E_\parallel\) since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.

ask.q: How is wave intensity \(I\) related to the emergent amplitude \(E_\parallel\)?
ask.why: The intensity of an electromagnetic wave is proportional to the square of its electric field amplitude.

steps.note: Multiply both sides by the intensity proportionality constant \(K\).
Replace \(K E_\parallel^2\) on the left with emergent intensity \(I\).

ask.q: What does \(K E_0^2\) represent when the two Polaroids are parallel (\(\theta = 0\))?
ask.why: When \(\theta = 0\), \(\cos\theta = 1\) and the emergent intensity is \(I_0 = K E_0^2\) (§22.2).

steps.note: Substitute \(I_0 = K E_0^2\) to obtain Malus's law (Eq. 22.9).

ask.q: According to Malus's law, what is \(I\) when \(\theta = 90^\circ\)?
ask.why: Since \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\), \(I = I_0\cos^2 90^\circ = 0\) (complete extinction).

cards.title: Parallel, 45-degree, and crossed Polaroids
cards.meaning: Crossed polarisers have their pass axes at 90° to each other, so the second sheet blocks all light transmitted by the first.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="34" width="70" height="96" rx="8" class="s ok"/><rect x="95" y="34" width="70" height="96" rx="8" class="s ok"/><rect x="176" y="34" width="70" height="96" rx="8" class="s ok"/><line x1="49" y1="48" x2="49" y2="116" class="lk"/><line x1="110" y1="104" x2="150" y2="60" class="lk"/><line x1="211" y1="48" x2="211" y2="116" class="gk"/><line x1="188" y1="82" x2="234" y2="82" class="ik"/><circle cx="211" cy="82" r="6" class="f"/><text x="49" y="26" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(a) θ = 0°</text><text x="49" y="148" text-anchor="middle" class="t">I = I₀ (100%)</text><text x="130" y="26" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(b) θ = 45°</text><text x="130" y="148" text-anchor="middle" class="t">I = I₀/2 (50%)</text><text x="211" y="26" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(c) θ = 90°</text><text x="211" y="148" text-anchor="middle" class="t">I = 0 (Dark)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare Fig. 22.7(a) parallel (full I₀), Fig. 22.7(b) at 45° (half intensity I₀/2), and Fig. 22.7(c) crossed at 90° (zero intensity).
cards.example: As you rotate P₂ through one full turn (0° to 360°), you see two bright maxima (0° and 180°) and two dark extinctions (90° and 270°).
cards.bridge: Either P₁ or P₂ can be rotated to produce the exact same cos²θ variation in transmitted intensity.

cards.label: 03 · §22.2 Definition
cards.title: What are crossed polarisers and how does rotation change intensity?
cards.body: Crossed polarisers have perpendicular pass axes (θ = 90°), giving zero transmitted intensity. Rotating one Polaroid through 360° produces two maxima (0°, 180°) and two zero minima (90°, 270°).

cards.label: 04 · §22.2 Intensity graph
cards.title: Malus's law intensity curve I = I₀ cos²θ
cards.body: As analyser angle θ varies from 0 to 2π, transmitted intensity I = I₀ cos²θ reaches maxima I₀ at θ = 0, π, 2π, equals 0.5 I₀ at θ = π/4, and drops to zero at θ = π/2 and 3π/2.

cards.label: 05 · §22.2 Worked example
cards.title: Transmitted intensity at θ = 45°, 60°, and 90° (§22.2)
cards.body: When two Polaroids are oriented at \(45^\circ\), \(\cos^2 45^\circ = 1/2\) so \(50\%\) of the linearly polarised intensity \(I_0\) passes through. At \(60^\circ\), \(25\%\) passes through, and at \(90^\circ\) no light passes through.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: How many times does intensity become zero when an analyser rotates through \(360^\circ\)?
cards.why: Since \(I = I_0\cos^2\theta\), complete extinction occurs twice per revolution at \(\theta = 90^\circ\) and \(\theta = 270^\circ\) (§22.2).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: When two Polaroids are oriented at \(45^\circ\), what fraction of \(I_0\) passes the second?

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Two Polaroids with their pass axes at \(90^\circ\) to each other are said to be ______.
cards.why: When two Polaroids have mutually perpendicular pass axes (\(\theta = 90^\circ\)), they are crossed and block all light (§22.2).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Polarised light of intensity \(100\text{ W/m}^2\) hits an analyser at \(\theta = 60^\circ\). Find emergent intensity in \(\text{W/m}^2\).
cards.why: From Malus's law, \(I = 100\cos^2 60^\circ = 100 \times (0.5)^2 = 25\text{ W/m}^2\).

sheets.title: Double refraction & Huygens
sheets.source: Unit 20 · Ghatak ch. 22 §22.5 (PDF pp. 365–368; Book 2 not available); syllabus item 20

cards.title: Why a calcite crystal shows a double image of a printed line
cards.meaning: Double refraction happens when an unpolarised beam enters an anisotropic crystal like calcite and splits into an ordinary ray (o-ray) and an extraordinary ray (e-ray).
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="84" y="34" width="84" height="112" class="s ok"/><line x1="18" y1="106" x2="84" y2="106" class="lk"/><line x1="84" y1="106" x2="226" y2="106" class="ik"/><line x1="84" y1="106" x2="168" y2="62" class="lk"/><line x1="168" y1="62" x2="226" y2="62" class="lk"/><line x1="96" y1="86" x2="156" y2="54" class="gk"/><circle cx="184" cy="106" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="204" cy="106" r="3" class="f"/><line x1="184" y1="52" x2="184" y2="72" class="lk"/><line x1="204" y1="52" x2="204" y2="72" class="lk"/><text x="126" y="26" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Calcite crystal</text><text x="126" y="134" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Optic axis (dashed)</text><text x="212" y="44" text-anchor="middle" class="t">e-ray (∥ plane)</text><text x="212" y="128" text-anchor="middle" class="t">o-ray (⊥ page)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at the unpolarised beam entering calcite (Fig. 22.20): the o-ray goes straight with dot vibrations, while the e-ray bends aside with bar vibrations.
cards.example: When you rotate the calcite crystal about the normal NN', the ordinary image stays fixed while the extraordinary image revolves around it!
cards.bridge: The o-ray always obeys Snell's law with D ⊥ optic axis (Eq. 22.43), while the e-ray has D in the plane containing k and the optic axis (Eq. 22.44).

cards.label: 01 · §22.5 Definition
cards.title: What are double refraction, the ordinary ray, and the extraordinary ray?
cards.body: Double refraction is the splitting of light in an anisotropic crystal into two linearly polarised rays: the ordinary ray (o-ray, obeys Snell's law, D ⊥ optic axis) and extraordinary ray (e-ray, D in optic-axis plane).

cards.title: Sphere and ellipsoid wavelets in negative and positive crystals
cards.meaning: The optic axis is the special direction in a uniaxial crystal along which the ordinary sphere and extraordinary ellipsoid touch because both rays have speed c/n_o.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="70" cy="90" r="32" class="ik"/><ellipse cx="70" cy="90" rx="32" ry="48" class="lk"/><line x1="24" y1="90" x2="116" y2="90" class="gk"/><circle cx="190" cy="90" r="46" class="ik"/><ellipse cx="190" cy="90" rx="46" ry="30" class="lk"/><line x1="136" y1="90" x2="244" y2="90" class="gk"/><text x="70" y="24" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(a) Negative (n_e < n_o)</text><text x="70" y="156" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Calcite: v_re(π/2) > v_ro</text><text x="190" y="24" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(b) Positive (n_e > n_o)</text><text x="190" y="156" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Quartz: v_re(π/2) < v_ro</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare Fig. 22.22(a) negative crystal (e-ray ellipsoid outside o-ray sphere) with Fig. 22.22(b) positive crystal (e-ray ellipsoid inside o-ray sphere).
cards.example: Along the horizontal optic axis (θ = 0), the sphere and ellipsoid touch at radius c/n_o; perpendicular to it (θ = π/2), the e-ray speed is c/n_e.
cards.bridge: Using Huygens' secondary wavelets with these spherical and ellipsoidal velocity surfaces explains double refraction at any angle of incidence.

cards.label: 02 · §22.5 Definition
cards.title: What are the optic axis, negative crystals, and positive crystals?
cards.body: The optic axis is the direction in a uniaxial crystal where o-ray and e-ray speeds equal c/n_o. In negative crystals (calcite, n_e < n_o) the e-ellipsoid lies outside the o-sphere; in positive (n_e > n_o) inside.

cards.label: 03 · §22.5 Derivation
cards.title: Extraordinary ray velocity surface and refractive index
cards.legend: Extraordinary ray velocity \(v_{re}(\theta)\) at angle \(\theta\) to the optic axis (\(z\)-axis), semi-axes \(a = c/n_o\) and \(b = c/n_e\), and ray refractive index \(n_{re} = c/v_{re}\) (Eqs. 22.37–22.45).

phases.name: Velocity law
phases.why: start from the extraordinary ray velocity equation at angle θ

phases.name: Polar ellipse
phases.why: set a = c/n_o, b = c/n_e, ρ = v_{re} and convert to Cartesian (z, x)

phases.name: Ray index
phases.why: multiply Eq. (22.37) by c² and substitute n_{re} = c / v_{re}

phases.name: Result
phases.why: take the square root to obtain the extraordinary ray refractive index

steps.note: Start from the extraordinary ray velocity equation at angle \(\theta\) to the optic axis (Eq. 22.37).
Set semi-axes \(a = c/n_o\), \(b = c/n_e\), and polar radius \(\rho = v_{re}\) (Eq. 22.39).

ask.q: Along the optic axis (\(\theta = 0\)), what does \(v_{re}\) equal?
ask.why: At \(\theta = 0\), \(\sin\theta = 0\) and \(\cos\theta = 1\), so \(v_{re} = c/n_o = v_{ro}\) (§22.5).

steps.note: Multiply both sides by \(\rho^2\).

ask.q: In polar coordinates \((\rho, \theta)\) around the \(z\)-axis, what are \(z\) and \(x\)?
ask.why: With \(\theta\) measured from the \(z\)-axis, \(z = \rho\cos\theta\) and \(x = \rho\sin\theta\) (§22.5).

steps.note: Thus plotting \(v_{re}(\theta)\) in 3D gives an ellipsoid of revolution (Eq. 22.38).

move.label: Multiply Eq. (22.37) by c²

steps.note: Multiply both sides of Eq. (22.37) by \(c^2\) to express \((c/v_{re})^2\).

ask.q: How is the extraordinary ray refractive index \(n_{re}\) defined?
ask.why: By definition (Eq. 22.45), the ray refractive index is \(n_{re} = c / v_{re}\).

steps.note: Substitute \(n_{re} = c / v_{re}\) on the left-hand side.

ask.q: Perpendicular to the optic axis (\(\theta = \pi/2\)), what does \(n_{re}\) equal?
ask.why: At \(\theta = \pi/2\), \(\cos\theta = 0\) and \(\sin\theta = 1\), so \(n_{re} = n_e\).

steps.note: Take the positive square root to get the extraordinary ray refractive index (Eq. 22.45).

cards.label: 04 · §§22.5.1–22.5.2 Huygens
cards.title: Huygens' construction for normal and oblique incidence (Figs. 22.23–22.25)
cards.body: Huygens' construction draws spheres of radius c/n_o (tangent OO' → o-ray BO) and ellipsoids of axes c/n_o, c/n_e (tangent EE' → e-ray BE). If the optic axis is parallel to the surface, both travel along BO.
examples: Axis ⊥ incidence: sin i/sin r = n_e

cards.label: 05 · §22.5 Worked comparison
cards.title: Negative vs positive uniaxial crystals perpendicular to the optic axis
cards.body: Perpendicular to the optic axis (\(\theta = \pi/2\)), the e-wave travels faster than the o-wave in a negative crystal like calcite (\(n_e = 1.486 < n_o = 1.658\)), and slower than the o-wave in a positive crystal like quartz (\(n_e = 1.553 > n_o = 1.544\)).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In a negative uniaxial crystal like calcite, how do \(n_e\) and \(n_o\) compare?
cards.why: In a negative crystal like calcite, \(n_e < n_o\), so perpendicular to the optic axis \(v_{re} = c/n_e > c/n_o = v_{ro}\) (Eq. 22.40).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: When light hits a crystal normally with the optic axis parallel to the surface:
options: The two rays split apart in angle
Both rays travel together at different speeds
Both rays travel at the same speed
cards.why: In Fig. 22.24(a,b), when the optic axis is parallel to the surface, both waves travel along the normal with different speeds \(c/n_o\) and \(c/n_e\) (§22.5.1).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Crystals like calcite and quartz that have only one optic axis are called ______ crystals.
cards.why: Crystals with a single direction along which the two rays have the same speed are called uniaxial crystals (§22.5).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Along the optic axis (\(\theta = 0^\circ\)), if \(n_o = 1.658\) and \(n_e = 1.486\), find \(n_{re}\).
cards.why: At \(\theta = 0^\circ\), \(n_{re} = \sqrt{n_o^2\cos^2 0^\circ + n_e^2\sin^2 0^\circ} = n_o = 1.658\) (Eq. 22.45).

sheets.title: Quarter-wave & half-wave plates

cards.title: Turning linear polarisation into a circle with a crystal plate
cards.meaning: A quarter-wave plate is a crystal slice cut parallel to its optic axis that delays one component by a quarter of a wavelength (phase π/2) behind the other.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="18" y1="90" x2="242" y2="90" class="gk"/><line x1="34" y1="122" x2="74" y2="58" class="lk"/><rect x="98" y="30" width="54" height="120" rx="6" class="s ok"/><line x1="112" y1="30" x2="112" y2="150" class="gk"/><line x1="125" y1="30" x2="125" y2="150" class="gk"/><line x1="138" y1="30" x2="138" y2="150" class="gk"/><circle cx="198" cy="90" r="32" class="lk"/><line x1="198" y1="90" x2="221" y2="67" class="ik"/><circle cx="221" cy="67" r="4" class="f"/><text x="54" y="46" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Linear (φ = 45°)</text><text x="125" y="22" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Calcite QWP (θ = π/2)</text><text x="125" y="166" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Optic axis ∥ surface</text><text x="198" y="46" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Circular (LCP)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at Fig. 22.26: linearly polarised light at φ = 45° enters a calcite QWP (optic axis parallel to surface) and emerges circularly polarised.
cards.example: Because φ = 45°, the o-wave (along x) and e-wave (along y) have equal amplitudes E₀/√2; a π/2 phase shift turns them into sin ωt and cos ωt.
cards.bridge: For a phase shift θ = (2m + 1)π/2, the required plate thickness is d = (2m + 1)λ₀ / [4(n_o - n_e)].

cards.label: 01 · §22.6 Definition
cards.title: What is a quarter-wave plate (QWP)?
cards.body: A quarter-wave plate is a uniaxial crystal plate with its optic axis parallel to the surface whose thickness d introduces a phase difference of π/2 (or (2m+1)π/2, path difference λ₀/4) between o- and e-waves.

cards.label: 02 · §22.6 Derivation
cards.title: Phase difference and thickness of a quarter-wave plate
cards.legend: Negative uniaxial crystal plate of thickness \(d\) with optic axis along \(y\), ordinary index \(n_o\), extraordinary index \(n_e\), and free-space wavenumber \(k = 2\pi / \lambda_0\) (Eqs. 22.50–22.53).

phases.name: Wave phases
phases.why: write the phases θ_o and θ_e accumulated across thickness d

phases.name: Phase lag
phases.why: subtract θ_e from θ_o and substitute k = 2π / λ₀

phases.name: Quarter wave
phases.why: set phase difference θ equal to an odd multiple (2m + 1)π/2

phases.name: Plate thickness
phases.why: solve for the QWP thickness d

steps.note: Inside a crystal of thickness \(d\), the \(x\)-component travels as an o-wave with phase \(\theta_o = n_o k d\).

move.label: Write phase of extraordinary wave at emerging surface

steps.note: The \(y\)-component (along the optic axis) travels as an e-wave with phase \(\theta_e = n_e k d\).

ask.q: How do we find the phase difference \(\theta\) between the o- and e-waves at \(z = d\)?
ask.why: The relative phase difference introduced by the crystal plate is \(\theta = \theta_o - \theta_e\) (Eq. 22.50).

steps.tex: \theta_o - \theta_e = n_o k d - n_e k d
steps.note: Subtract \(\theta_e\) from \(\theta_o\).
Set \(\theta = \theta_o - \theta_e\) and factor out \(kd\) (Eq. 22.50).

ask.q: How is the free-space wavenumber \(k\) related to wavelength \(\lambda_0\)?
ask.why: In free space, \(k = \omega / c = 2\pi / \lambda_0\).

steps.note: Replace \(k\) with \(2\pi / \lambda_0\) to relate phase difference \(\theta\) to path difference \((n_o - n_e)d\).

ask.q: For a quarter-wave plate (QWP), what phase difference \(\theta\) is required?
ask.why: A quarter-wave plate introduces an odd multiple of \(\pi/2\), i.e., \(\theta = (2m + 1)\pi/2\) (Eq. 22.53).

steps.note: Set \(\theta = (2m + 1)\pi/2\) for a general quarter-wave plate (Eq. 22.53).
Multiply both sides by \(\lambda_0 / [2\pi(n_o - n_e)]\); the factor \(\pi\) cancels.

ask.q: For \(m = 0\), what is the minimum thickness \(d\) of a calcite QWP?
ask.why: Setting \(m = 0\) in Eq. (22.53) gives the minimum QWP thickness \(d = \lambda_0 / [4(n_o - n_e)]\) (Eq. 22.52).

steps.note: Swap sides to obtain the quarter-wave plate thickness formula (Eq. 22.53).

cards.title: Flipping one electric component to rotate a plane wave by 90°
cards.meaning: A half-wave plate delays one component by half a wavelength (phase π), which reverses its sign and flips the polarisation across the optic axis.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="18" y1="90" x2="242" y2="90" class="gk"/><line x1="34" y1="124" x2="74" y2="56" class="lk"/><rect x="98" y="30" width="58" height="120" rx="6" class="s ok"/><line x1="114" y1="30" x2="114" y2="150" class="gk"/><line x1="127" y1="30" x2="127" y2="150" class="gk"/><line x1="140" y1="30" x2="140" y2="150" class="gk"/><line x1="182" y1="56" x2="222" y2="124" class="ik"/><text x="54" y="44" text-anchor="middle" class="t">In: +45° to y</text><text x="127" y="22" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Calcite HWP (θ = π)</text><text x="127" y="166" text-anchor="middle" class="t">E_x → -E_x, E_y → +E_y</text><text x="202" y="44" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Out: 135° (rot 90°)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at Fig. 22.27: a linearly polarised wave at +45° to the y-axis has E_x reversed by the HWP, rotating the polarisation by 90° to 135°.
cards.example: Because cos(ωt - π) = -cos ωt, the x-component flips sign while the y-component stays +cos ωt.
cards.bridge: Similarly, a HWP turns left-circularly polarised light (LCP) into right-circularly polarised light (RCP), and vice versa.

cards.label: 03 · §22.6 Definition
cards.title: What is a half-wave plate (HWP)?
cards.body: A half-wave plate is a crystal plate with optic axis parallel to the surface that introduces a phase difference of π (path difference λ₀/2). It rotates linear polarisation at angle φ by 2φ and flips LCP to RCP.
cards.tex: d = (2m + 1)\frac{\lambda_0}{2|n_o - n_e|}, \quad E_x = -\frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\omega t, \quad E_y = \frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\omega t

cards.label: 04 · §22.6 Examples 22.6–22.8
cards.title: Worked example: calcite QWP thickness and emergent states
cards.body: For calcite at \(\lambda_0 = 5893\text{ \AA}\) (\(n_o = 1.65836, n_e = 1.48641\)), minimum QWP thickness is \(0.000857\text{ mm}\) (Example 22.6). A calcite crystal of thickness \(0.005141\text{ mm}\) gives \(\theta = 3\pi\), acting as a HWP that converts LCP into RCP (Example 22.7).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Linearly polarised light at \(45^\circ\) to the optic axis passes through a QWP. It emerges:
cards.why: At \(\phi = 45^\circ\), the two orthogonal components have equal amplitudes and a \(\pi/2\) phase shift, producing circularly polarised light (Eq. 22.51).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What does a half-wave plate (HWP) do to left-circularly polarised (LCP) light?
cards.why: A phase shift of \(\pi\) reverses one component (\(\sin(\omega t - \pi) = -\sin\omega t\)), converting LCP into RCP (Example 22.7).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: If phase difference \(\theta\) is not a multiple of \(\pi/2\), the emergent beam is ______ polarised.
cards.why: When \(\theta \neq \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2, 2\pi, \dots\), the superposition of the o- and e-waves is elliptically polarised (§22.6).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: For \(\lambda_0 = 600\text{ nm}\) and \(|n_o - n_e| = 0.15\), find minimum QWP thickness \(d\) in \(\mu\text{m}\).
cards.why: \(d = \frac{\lambda_0}{4|n_o - n_e|} = \frac{0.6\,\mu\text{m}}{4 \times 0.15} = \frac{0.6}{0.6} = 1\,\mu\text{m}\).

sheets.title: Analysis & optical activity
sheets.source: Unit 22 · Ghatak ch. 22 §§22.7–22.8 (PDF pp. 372–375; Book 2 not available); syllabus item 22

cards.title: Telling all seven states of polarisation apart with a Polaroid and QWP
cards.meaning: To the human eye all polarisations look the same, so we first rotate a single Polaroid and then insert a quarter-wave plate if needed.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="14" width="72" height="152" rx="8" class="s ok"/><rect x="94" y="14" width="72" height="152" rx="8" class="s ok"/><rect x="176" y="14" width="72" height="152" rx="8" class="s ok"/><text x="48" y="34" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(i) Zero min</text><text x="48" y="76" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Polaroid</text><text x="48" y="94" text-anchor="middle" class="t">alone gives</text><text x="48" y="112" text-anchor="middle" class="t">2 dark zeros</text><text x="48" y="148" text-anchor="middle" class="t">→ Linear</text><text x="130" y="34" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(ii) Constant</text><text x="130" y="68" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Add QWP:</text><text x="130" y="92" text-anchor="middle" class="t">0 min → Circ</text><text x="130" y="114" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Const → Unpol</text><text x="130" y="136" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Var → Mix</text><text x="212" y="34" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(iii) Varies</text><text x="212" y="68" text-anchor="middle" class="t">QWP ∥ I_max:</text><text x="212" y="92" text-anchor="middle" class="t">0 min → Ellip</text><text x="212" y="114" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Same → Lin+U</text><text x="212" y="136" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Shift → Ell+U</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare the three outcomes of rotating a Polaroid (§22.7): (i) two zero minima → linear; (ii) constant → test with QWP; (iii) varies without zero → align QWP with I_max.
cards.example: Circularly polarised light and unpolarised light both give constant intensity through a rotating Polaroid, but a QWP turns circular light into linear light (giving two zero minima)!
cards.bridge: Similarly, aligning a QWP with the maximum-intensity axis turns pure elliptically polarised light into linearly polarised light.

cards.label: 01 · §22.7 Definition
cards.title: What is the procedure for analysis of polarised light?
cards.body: Rotating a Polaroid gives extinction for linear light, constant intensity for unpolarised or circular light, and partial variation for elliptical or mixed light. Adding a QWP distinguishes circular and elliptical states.

cards.title: Why sugar solution and quartz twist the plane of polarisation
cards.meaning: Optical activity is the steady rotation of the plane of linear polarisation because the medium's left-circular (LCP) and right-circular (RCP) modes travel at slightly different speeds.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="48" cy="88" r="28" class="lk"/><circle cx="124" cy="88" r="28" class="ik"/><line x1="48" y1="88" x2="34" y2="64" class="lk"/><line x1="124" y1="88" x2="148" y2="74" class="ik"/><line x1="210" y1="34" x2="210" y2="142" class="gk"/><line x1="176" y1="88" x2="244" y2="88" class="gk"/><line x1="188" y1="126" x2="232" y2="50" class="lk"/><path d="M 210 56 A 32 32 0 0 1 226 60" class="lk"/><text x="48" y="38" text-anchor="middle" class="t">RCP (φ₁ = k_R z)</text><text x="86" y="92" text-anchor="middle" class="t">+</text><text x="124" y="38" text-anchor="middle" class="t">LCP (φ₂ = k_L z)</text><text x="164" y="92" text-anchor="middle" class="t">=</text><text x="210" y="24" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Rotated LP (φ)</text><text x="130" y="164" text-anchor="middle" class="t">φ(z) = ½(k_L - k_R)z = (π/λ)(n_L - n_R)z</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at Fig. 22.28: adding RCP (rotated by φ₁ = k_R z) and LCP (rotated by φ₂ = k_L z) produces a linearly polarised wave rotated by φ = ½(φ₂ - φ₁).
cards.example: In a sugar solution, the rotation angle φ is proportional to both tube length z and sugar concentration, which industry uses to measure sugar content.
cards.bridge: If n_L > n_R (φ > 0), the medium is right-handed (dextro-rotatory); if n_L < n_R (φ < 0), it is left-handed (laevo-rotatory).

cards.label: 02 · §22.8 Definition
cards.title: What is optical activity?
cards.body: Optical activity is the rotation of the plane of polarisation by φ(z) = (π/λ)(n_L - n_R)z because LCP and RCP modes have different indices n_L and n_R. Dextro-rotatory media have n_L > n_R; laevo-rotatory have n_L < n_R.

cards.label: 03 · §22.8 Derivation
cards.title: Rotation of plane of polarisation in an optically active medium
cards.legend: Superposition of RCP wave (\(k_R = \frac{\omega}{c}n_R\)) and LCP wave (\(k_L = \frac{\omega}{c}n_L\)) propagating along \(+z\), with \(\theta(z) = \frac{1}{2}(k_L + k_R)z\) (Eqs. 22.56–22.58, Fig. 22.28).

phases.name: Superpose x
phases.why: add the x-components of the RCP and LCP waves

phases.name: Superpose y
phases.why: add the y-components of the RCP and LCP waves

phases.name: Rotation angle
phases.why: divide E_y by E_x to find the rotation angle φ(z)

phases.name: Refractive indices
phases.why: substitute k_L = 2πn_L/λ and k_R = 2πn_R/λ

steps.tex: E_x = E_0[\cos(k_R z - \omega t) + \cos(k_L z - \omega t)]
steps.note: Add the \(x\)-components of the RCP wave (Eq. 22.56) and LCP wave (Eq. 22.57).
Combine the two cosines, where \(\theta(z) = \frac{1}{2}(k_L + k_R)z\).

ask.q: At \(z = 0\), what are \(E_x\) and \(E_y\) when the RCP and LCP waves add?
ask.why: At \(z = 0\), the \(y\)-components \(-\sin(-\omega t)\) and \(+\sin(-\omega t)\) cancel, leaving linear polarisation along \(x\).

move.label: Add y-components of RCP and LCP waves (Eqs. 22.56–22.57)

steps.tex: E_y = E_0[-\sin(k_R z - \omega t) + \sin(k_L z - \omega t)]
steps.note: Add the \(y\)-components \(E_y^R\) and \(E_y^L\) after propagating distance \(z\).
Both \(E_x\) and \(E_y\) oscillate in phase as \(\cos[\omega t - \theta(z)]\), so the wave stays linearly polarised.

ask.q: Since \(E_x\) and \(E_y\) oscillate in phase, how is the rotation angle \(\phi(z)\) found?
ask.why: For a vector with components \((E_x, E_y)\), the angle \(\phi(z)\) with the \(x\)-axis satisfies \(\tan\phi(z) = E_y / E_x\).

move.label: Divide E_y by E_x to get tan φ(z)

steps.note: Dividing \(E_y\) by \(E_x\) cancels \(2E_0\cos[\omega t - \theta(z)]\).
Equate the angles inside the tangent.

ask.q: What replaces \(k_L - k_R\) in terms of free-space wavelength \(\lambda\)?
ask.why: Since \(k_L = (2\pi/\lambda)n_L\) and \(k_R = (2\pi/\lambda)n_R\), \(k_L - k_R = (2\pi/\lambda)(n_L - n_R)\).

steps.note: This gives the angle of optical rotation after distance \(z\) (Eq. 22.58).

ask.q: In an isotropic medium where \(n_L = n_R\), what is the rotation angle \(\phi(z)\)?
ask.why: When \(n_L = n_R\), \(\phi(z) = 0\) and the plane of polarisation does not rotate (§22.8).

cards.label: 04 · §22.8 Worked example
cards.title: Worked example: optical rotation in quartz and turpentine (§22.8)
cards.body: For linearly polarised light (\(\lambda_0 = 0.6\,\mu\text{m} = 6000\text{ \AA}\)) propagating along the optic axis of quartz, \(|n_L - n_R| \approx 7\times 10^{-5}\), giving \(\phi = 21^\circ\) in \(z = 0.1\text{ cm}\) (\(1\text{ mm}\)). For turpentine, \(\phi = +37^\circ\) for \(z = 10\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Rotating a Polaroid gives constant intensity, then adding a QWP gives extinction. The beam is:
cards.why: A QWP converts circularly polarised light into linearly polarised light, which then shows two zero minima through the rotating Polaroid (§22.7).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In an optically active medium, when is the substance dextro-rotatory (right-handed)?
cards.why: By Eq. (22.58), \(\phi(z) = (\pi/\lambda)(n_L - n_R)z > 0\) (dextro-rotatory) when \(n_L > n_R\) (§22.8).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: The normal modes of propagation in an optically active medium are LCP and ______ waves.
cards.why: In an optically active medium, the normal modes that propagate unchanged in polarisation state are LCP and RCP waves (§22.8).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A quartz plate rotates polarisation by \(21^\circ\) per mm at \(6000\text{ \AA}\). Find rotation in degrees for \(3\text{ mm}\).
cards.why: Since optical rotation \(\phi(z)\) is directly proportional to thickness \(z\), \(\phi = 3 \times 21^\circ = 63^\circ\) (§22.8).
